title: Commands
content:
The framework installs the command vendor/bin/wp-app-framework into your project. It runs in the project whose vendor/autoload.php it loads, which is the project you call it in.

Command	Does
build [--output=<file>]	Builds and checks the manifest of the project: services, hooks, routes, blocks and their templates, parts and patterns. Without --output it writes nothing; with it, it writes a release manifest. Exit code 1 with a list of errors. See Build.
release [--output=<zip>] [--expect-version=<version>] [--package-source=<package>=<directory>]...	Builds the release ZIP: copies the project, installs the dependencies, prefixes them with Strauss, builds the manifest and the scripts and checks the result. --expect-version fails if the version in the header differs; --package-source builds with a local checkout of a package. See Release.
meta-fields <meta class> [--force]	Writes the class with #[MetaFields] for a meta class, next to it. See Queries.
table-fields <row class> [--force]	Writes the class with #[TableFields] for a row class, next to it. See Tables.

Options take their value with =: --output=dist/theme.zip. meta-fields and table-fields replace an existing file only with --force; they are the only commands that write source code.

Your project usually runs them through Composer scripts, for example "build-manifest": "wp-app-framework build" and "release": "wp-app-framework release" (see Getting started).

title: composer.json
description: The framework reads these keys of the composer.json of your theme or plugin. Nothing else is configured there; everything else is code. A minimal theme: Getting started shows the complete file with the Strauss settings and scripts.

title: Hooks
content:
The framework fires these WordPress hooks. The {slug} is the directory name of the theme or plugin, {namespace} its namespace (see Concepts).

Hook	Kind	Arguments	Use
wp_app_framework/init/{slug}	action	none	Fired at the end of the boot of an instance. Use it to run code once the framework of a theme or plugin is ready. See Boot.
wp_app_framework/namespace/{namespace}	action	none	Fired when an instance claims its namespace; a second instance with the same namespace stops with an error. Not meant for your code.
wp_app_framework/api/{slug}	filter	null, the class name	The public API of a plugin or theme (#[PublicApi]). The framework uses it to resolve #[PluginApi] and #[ThemeApi] parameters; do not call it yourself. See Plugins.
wp_app_framework/template/{slug}	filter	null, 'function' or 'filter', the name	The public Twig functions and filters of a plugin or theme (public: true). The framework uses it in templates of other instances; do not call it yourself. See Plugins.
wp_app_framework/cache/backends/{slug}	filter	the list of backends	The cache backends of an instance, in order of preference: 'object', 'file', 'transient'; [] turns the cache off. See Cache.
wp_app_framework/cron/{slug}/{name}	action (WP-Cron)	none	A recurring event (#[CronEvent]). See Cron events and tasks.
wp_app_framework/cron/{slug}/task/{name}	action (WP-Cron)	the data of the task	A one-time task (#[CronTask]); the framework turns the data back into the task object.
wp_app_framework/cache/clean_up/{slug}	action (WP-Cron)	none	The daily clean-up of the file cache and of Twig caches of older releases.

The names and arguments of init, namespace, api and template are a contract between framework versions: instances built with different versions of the framework meet on them, so they only ever grow, also across major versions.

The run-time hooks of WordPress the framework uses itself (init, enqueue_block_assets, rest_api_init …) are not part of its API.

title: API reference
content:
This part of the documentation lists everything your theme or plugin can use: each attribute, class, Twig function and JavaScript export on a page of its own, with its parameters, types and defaults. The guides explain how the parts work together and why; come here when you need the exact signature.

The pages are generated from the code of the framework and its doc comments, so they always match the version you read the documentation for.

What belongs to the API

The API is what this reference lists. Within a major version it only grows: nothing listed here is renamed, removed or changed in behavior (see Upgrading).

Everything else in the framework is internal, even if PHP lets you reach it: classes that are not listed, public methods marked @internal in the code, and the parts of the JavaScript global window.wpAppFramework[slug] other than api and view. Internal code can change in any version. Injecting one of the framework's internal services into a class of your own is a build error.

Sections

Attributes declare blocks, values, hooks, REST routes, settings, post types, tables, cache, cron, WP-CLI commands, lifecycle methods and Twig functions.

Boot classes start the framework in a theme, child theme or plugin and describe it.

Services are provided by the framework: inject them like your own.

Posts and queries, Query fields and Tables are the active records and their queries.

Cache lists the tags and variants of cached entries.

Values and exceptions are value objects, interfaces you implement and exceptions you throw.

Enums are the cases attributes and queries take.

Twig functions are available in every template, the framework's own and the wrappers of WordPress functions. Besides them, templates have the global settings with your settings groups.

JavaScript lists the exports of @saij/wp-app-framework for editor scripts and of @saij/wp-app-framework/view for view scripts.

Configuration and commands covers what is not code: hooks, composer.json, commands, the webpack helper and the release workflow.

title: #[PluginApi]
content:
Attribute on parameters.

use Saij\WpAppFramework\Api\PluginApi;

Injects the public API (#[PublicApi]) of a plugin into a constructor
parameter of a service: #[PluginApi('my-plugin')] ?NoteApi $notes = null.

The parameter must be nullable with the default null: it receives null if
the plugin is not active. The class is not loaded by the build, so the plugin
may be missing; require it as a development dependency for the IDE and static
analysis. Resolving the service before plugins_loaded is an error, because
not all plugins are loaded then.

Arguments

#[PluginApi(string $plugin)]

Parameter	Type	Default	Description
plugin	string	required	Slug of the plugin (its directory name).
description: Attribute on parameters. Injects the public API (#[PublicApi]) of a plugin into a constructor parameter of a service: #[PluginApi('my-plugin')] ?NoteApi $notes = null. The parameter must be nullable with the default null: it receives null if the plugin is not active. The class is not loaded by the build, so the plugin may be missing; require it as a development dependency for the IDE and static analysis. Resolving the service before plugins_loaded is an error, because not all plugins are loaded then.

title: #[PublicApi]
content:
Attribute on classes.

use Saij\WpAppFramework\Api\PublicApi;

Marks a service of a plugin or theme as its public API: other consumers of
the framework receive it through a constructor parameter with #[PluginApi]
(the API of a plugin) or #[ThemeApi] (child themes, the API of their parent).

Plugins and themes declare public APIs, child themes do not. The service is
created when a consumer first needs it. Its public methods and the project
classes they use must not use classes of the framework or of other
dependencies: a release prefixes them, so their names differ in every
consumer (build error). The provider keeps its API compatible itself.
description: Attribute on classes. Plugins and themes declare public APIs, child themes do not. The service is created when a consumer first needs it. Its public methods and the project classes they use must not use classes of the framework or of other dependencies: a release prefixes them, so their names differ in every consumer (build error). The provider keeps its API compatible itself.

title: #[ThemeApi]
content:
Attribute on parameters.

use Saij\WpAppFramework\Api\ThemeApi;

Injects the public API (#[PublicApi]) of the parent theme into a
constructor parameter of a service of a child theme:
#[ThemeApi] ?SectionsApi $sections = null.

Only child themes use it; the parent theme is the one named by the
Template: header of their style.css. The parameter must be nullable with
the default null, like #[PluginApi]. The class is not loaded by the build;
require the parent theme as a development dependency for the IDE and static
analysis. Resolving the service before after_setup_theme is an error,
because the parent theme boots after the child theme.
description: Attribute on parameters. Injects the public API (#[PublicApi]) of the parent theme into a constructor parameter of a service of a child theme: #[ThemeApi] ?SectionsApi $sections = null. Only child themes use it; the parent theme is the one named by the Template: header of their style.css. The parameter must be nullable with the default null, like #[PluginApi]. The class is not loaded by the build; require the parent theme as a development dependency for the IDE and static analysis. Resolving the service before after_setup_theme is an error, because the parent theme boots after the child theme.

title: Assets
content: Class. use Saij\WpAppFramework\Asset\Assets; The static files of the instance's assets/ directory: their URL, path, an element or an inline SVG. The Twig functions asset_url(), asset_image() and asset_svg() call this service; inject it where PHP needs a file, for example in a pattern or a mail. An asset is named by its path below assets/, e.g. images/logo.svg. A higher layer replaces it with a file of the same name in its overrides directory: a child theme in overrides/{theme}/assets/, a theme or child theme in overrides/{plugin}/assets/. @child/… names a file of the active child theme's own assets/ directory, which needs no counterpart in the theme; @theme/… or @plugin/… names the instance's own file and ignores overrides. Constants Constant Value Description CHILD_PREFIX '@child/' Prefix of the files of the active child theme's own asset directory. Methods image() image(string $name, string $alt, array $attributes = []): string An element for an image: src, width and height (so the page does not jump while it loads), alt, decoding="async" and further attributes. With widths and sizes the element gets a srcset of smaller versions; with formats (e.g. ['avif', 'webp']) it is wrapped in a with a per format. The build creates these variants from the literal calls of asset_image() in the templates. Parameter Type Default Description name string required The asset: its path below assets/, e.g. images/logo.svg, optionally with @child/ or the prefix of the instance (@theme/, @plugin/). alt string required The alternative text; '' for a decorative image. attributes array|list> [] Further attributes; true adds one without value, false leaves it out. widths (list of pixel widths) and formats ask for variants and then need sizes; src, alt and srcset cannot be set. Returns string Throws InvalidArgumentException: If the name is invalid or names no asset, or an attribute is invalid. Throws LogicException: If the variants the attributes ask for were not built, or the name starts with @child/ but no child theme is active. path() path(string $name): string The path of an asset in the file system. Parameter Type Default Description name string required The asset: its path below assets/, e.g. images/logo.svg, optionally with @child/ or the prefix of the instance (@theme/, @plugin/). Returns string Throws InvalidArgumentException: If the name is invalid or names no asset. Throws LogicException: If the name starts with @child/ but no child theme is active. svg() svg(string $name, array $attributes = []): string The markup of an SVG image, to place it inline (for example icons styled with CSS), with further attributes on its root element; classes are added to its own. Parameter Type Default Description name string required The asset: its path below assets/, e.g. images/logo.svg, optionally with @child/ or the prefix of the instance (@theme/, @plugin/). The file must have the extension .svg. attributes array [] Attributes to set on the root element; true sets one without value, false removes it. class adds its classes to those of the file. Returns string Throws InvalidArgumentException: If the asset is no SVG image or has no root element
description: Class. The static files of the instance's assets/ directory: their URL, path, an element or an inline SVG. The Twig functions asset_url(), asset_image() and asset_svg() call this service; inject it where PHP needs a file, for example in a pattern or a mail. An asset is named by its path below assets/, e.g. images/logo.svg. A higher layer replaces it with a file of the same name in its overrides directory: a child theme in overrides/{theme}/assets/, a theme or child theme in overrides/{plugin}/assets/. @child/… names a file of the active child theme's own assets/ directory, which needs no counterpart in the theme; @theme/… or @plugin/… names the instance's own file and ignores overrides.

title: MediaLibrary
content:
Class.

use Saij\WpAppFramework\Asset\MediaLibrary;

Imports static assets of the instance into the media library, for content
that needs attachments: an #[Image] field takes the ID of an attachment,
not a file of the theme. Call it where content is created, for example in a
method with #[OnActivation] or in a WP-CLI command.

The import is idempotent per site: an asset already imported with the same
content returns its attachment. A changed file becomes a new attachment; the
old one stays, because content may use it. Attachments stay in the media
library when the theme or plugin is removed.

Returns int: The ID of the attachment.

Throws InvalidArgumentException: If the name names no asset of the instance.

Throws RuntimeException: If WordPress cannot store the file or create the attachment.

use Saij\WpAppFramework\Cache\CacheStore;

The cache of a theme or plugin. Inject it to cache data of your own, for
example the response of an external API:

$weather = $this->cache->remember('weather', fn(): array => $this->client->fetch(), ttl: 600, tags: [Feed::Weather]);

Blocks and REST routes with #[Cache] use the same cache. Entries are stored
in the first available backend of the filter
wp_app_framework/cache/backends/{slug} (default: object cache, files,
transients).

Methods

getBackendName()

The backend that stores the entries in this request ("object", "file" or "transient"); null if caching is off.

Returns ?string

Invalidates the tags: entries with one of them are never read again.

Parameter	Type	Default	Description
...tags	CacheTag		The tags to invalidate, in the cache of this theme or plugin.

Throws InvalidArgumentException: If a tag is invalid, e.g. names an unknown post class.

remember()

remember(string $key, Closure $compute, int $ttl, array $tags = [], array $vary = []): mixed

Returns the cached value of the key, or computes, stores and returns it.

Values must be plain data: null, booleans, numbers, strings and arrays of them. Exceptions of $compute are passed

title: ChildTheme
content:
Class.

use Saij\WpAppFramework\ChildTheme;

Boots the framework for an active child theme with code of its own and
provides its paths.

A child theme with blocks, hooks or routes is a framework instance of its
own: its slug is get_stylesheet(), its release prefixes its own copy of the
framework, and it talks to its parent theme only through the public API
(#[ThemeApi]) and public template callables of the parent. A child theme
that only overrides templates of its parent (overrides/{parent}/) needs no
boot and no build.

The instance is created only by boot() and handed to the container as a
predefined instance: services of the child theme can inject it.

Boots the framework. Called once from the child theme's functions.php,
which WordPress loads before the parent theme's.

Release mode applies if the child theme contains generated/manifest.php
(created only by the release build). Caches live in
wp-content/cache/{stylesheet}. Templates are looked up in the child
theme's src/, then in the framework. At its end, boot() fires the action
wp_app_framework/init/{stylesheet}.

A child theme with blocks, hooks or routes is a framework instance of its own: its slug is get_stylesheet(), its release prefixes its own copy of the framework, and it talks to its parent theme only through the public API (#[ThemeApi]) and public template callables of the parent. A child theme that only overrides templates of its parent (overrides/{parent}/) needs no boot and no build. The instance is created only by boot() and handed to the container as a predefined instance: services of the child theme can inject it.

title: #[CronEvent]
content:
Attribute on methods.

use Saij\WpAppFramework\Cron\CronEvent;

Runs a public method of a service as a recurring WP-Cron event.

The method returns void; its parameters are services, because WP-Cron passes
no arguments to recurring events. The event is scheduled on the first request,
rescheduled when the interval, at or weekday changes and unscheduled when
the method loses the attribute. Its hook is wp_app_framework/cron/{slug}/{name}.

$interval is a CronInterval or a number of seconds (at least 60). Write the
number itself (15 * 60): attribute arguments are evaluated in the build,
where WordPress constants such as MINUTE_IN_SECONDS do not exist.

$at (HH:MM, in the time zone of the site) fixes the start time of daily,
twice daily and weekly events; weekly events with $at also need $weekday.

Arguments

#[CronEvent(string $name, CronInterval|int $interval, ?string $at = null, ?Weekday $weekday = null)]

Parameter	Type	Default	Description
name	string	required	Lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, starting with a letter; unique among the events of the theme or plugin.
interval	CronInterval|int	required	A WordPress interval or seconds, at least 60.
at	string|null	null	Start time HH:MM in the time zone of the site.
weekday	Weekday|null	null	Day of weekly events with $at.
description: Attribute on methods. Runs a public method of a service as a recurring WP-Cron event. The method returns void; its parameters are services, because WP-Cron passes no arguments to recurring events. The event is scheduled on the first request, rescheduled when the interval, at or weekday changes and unscheduled when the method loses the attribute. Its hook is wp_app_framework/cron/{slug}/{name}. $interval is a CronInterval or a number of seconds (at least 60). Write the number itself (15 * 60): attribute arguments are evaluated in the build, where WordPress constants such as MINUTE_IN_SECONDS do not exist. $at (HH:MM, in the time zone of the site) fixes the start time of daily, twice daily and weekly events; weekly events with $at also need $weekday.

title: CronScheduler
content:
Class.

use Saij\WpAppFramework\Cron\CronScheduler;

Schedules one-time WP-Cron tasks of the theme or plugin. Inject it into a
service:

$this->cron->schedule(new SendReminder($postId), new DateTimeImmutable('+1 hour'));

A task is an object of a value class with a #[CronTask] handler. Two tasks
are the same if their values are equal: WP-Cron stores the values of the task
as the argument of the event and finds, compares and unschedules events by
their arguments.

Methods

isScheduled()

isScheduled(object $task): bool

Whether a task equal to the given one is scheduled.

Parameter	Type	Default	Description
task	object	required	The task: an object of a value class that is the first parameter of a #[CronTask] handler of this theme or plugin. Equal to the task to look for: same class, equal values.

Returns bool

Throws LogicException: If the task has no #[CronTask] handler in this theme or plugin.

schedule()

schedule(object $task, DateTimeInterface $at): bool

Schedules the task to run at the given time (or on the next request after it).

Parameter	Type	Default	Description
task	object	required	The task: an object of a value class that is the first parameter of a #[CronTask] handler of this theme or plugin.
at	DateTimeInterface	required	The time to run the task, in any time zone.

Returns bool: True if scheduled, false if WordPress already has the same task within 10 minutes of that time.

Throws RuntimeException: If WordPress refuses the task for another reason (e.g. a time before 1970, or a plugin).

Throws LogicException: If the task has no #[CronTask] handler in this theme or plugin.

unschedule()

unschedule(object $task): int

Removes every scheduled task equal to the given one.

Parameter	Type	Default	Description
task	object	required	The task: an object of a value class that is the first parameter of a #[CronTask] handler of this theme or plugin. Equal to the task to remove: same class, equal values.

Returns int: The number of tasks removed.

Throws RuntimeException: If WordPress cannot save the cron events.

Throws LogicException: If the task has no #[CronTask] handler in this theme or plugin.
description: Class. Schedules one-time WP-Cron tasks of the theme or plugin. Inject it into a service: A task is an object of a value class with a #[CronTask] handler. Two tasks are the same if their values are equal: WP-Cron stores the values of the task as the argument of the event and finds, compares and unschedules events by their arguments.

A post object is loaded with Event::get($id) or Event::find($id) and created

A post object is loaded with Event::get($id) or Event::find($id) and created with new Event(). title: #[PostMeta]
content:
Attribute on classes.

use Saij\WpAppFramework\Post\PostMeta;

Declares a class of post meta fields: each promoted constructor parameter is a
field, stored in its own meta key {namespace}_{field} (field name in snake
case). The fields are reached through the post object only:
$event->meta(EventDetails::class).

The class is not readonly: the fields are usually private, with getters and
setters, and save() of the post writes the changed values.

postTypes	list<class-string<AbstractPost>>	required	Post classes the fields belong to: classes with #[PostType], Post or Page.
description: Attribute on classes. Declares a class of post meta fields: each promoted constructor parameter is a field, stored in its own meta key {namespace}_{field} (field name in snake case). title: #[PostType]
content:
Attribute on classes.

use Saij\WpAppFramework\Post\PostType;

Declares a post type on a subclass of AbstractPost: the class is the object of a
post of the type. The framework registers the type as {namespace}_{name}
(namespace of the theme or plugin with "_" instead of "-"), always shown in the
REST API and therefore in the block editor if it supports the editor.

Arguments

#[PostType(string $name, string $label, string $singularLabel, ?PostTypeLabels $labels = null, string $description = '', bool $public = true, bool $showUi = true, array $supports = [PostTypeSupport::Title, PostTypeSupport::Editor], bool $hierarchical = false, bool $archive = false, ?string $slug = null, ?string $menuIcon = null, ?int $menuPosition = null)]

Parameter	Type	Default	Description
name	string	required	Name without namespace: lowercase letters, digits and "_", starting with a letter; the full name has at most 20 characters.
label	string	required	Plural name, e.g. "Events".
singularLabel	string	required	Singular name, e.g. "Event".
labels	PostTypeLabels|null	null	Further labels; null derives all of them from the names in English.
description	string	''	Description of the post type.
public	bool	true	The type is shown on the front end and in searches; false for data without pages of its own. Unlike in WordPress, true by default.
showUi	bool	true	The type has screens and a menu entry in the admin.
supports	list<PostTypeSupport>	[PostTypeSupport::Title, PostTypeSupport::Editor]	Features of the type; custom-fields is added for meta.
hierarchical	bool	false	Posts have parents, like pages.
archive	bool	false	The type has an archive page at its slug.
slug	string|null	null	URL slug; null uses the name with "-" instead of "_".
menuIcon	string|null	null	Dashicon class or URL of the admin menu icon.
menuPosition	int|null	null	Position in the admin menu (WordPress' menu_position); null puts it below Comments.
description: Attribute on classes. Declares a post type on a subclass of AbstractPost: the class is the object of a post of the type. The framework registers the type as {namespace}_{name} (namespace of the theme or plugin with "_" instead of "-"), always shown in the REST API and therefore in the block editor if it supports the editor.

title: Field
content:
Abstract class.

use Saij\WpAppFramework\Query\Field\Field;

A field of a meta class or a column of a table in queries: its methods create conditions, and the query sorts by
it. Created by the static methods of a class with #[MetaFields] or #[TableFields]; the subclass matches the type of
the field.

A meta value that is not stored counts as the default of its constructor parameter, in conditions and in the
sort order. Columns of a table are compared as stored; see the Nullable… field classes for null.

Methods

The class the field belongs to.

Returns class-string

The name of the field: the name of the constructor parameter.

Returns string
description: Abstract class. A field of a meta class or a column of a table in queries: its methods create conditions, and the query sorts by it. Created by the static methods of a class with #[MetaFields] or #[TableFields]; the subclass matches the type of the field. A meta value that is not stored counts as the default of its constructor parameter, in conditions and in the sort order. Columns of a table are compared as stored; see the Nullable… field classes for null.

title: PostQuery
content:
Class.

use Saij\WpAppFramework\Query\PostQuery;

A query for posts of a post class, started with Event::query(), run through WP_Query and returning post objects.

A query never changes: every method returns a changed copy, so a query can be passed on and varied safely. Keep
the result – $query->limit(3); alone does nothing, and PHP warns about it (#[\NoDiscard]).

$events = Event::query()
    ->where(EventDetailsFields::capacity()->greaterThan(10))
    ->where(Terms::in(Genre::class, [$jazz]))
    ->orderBy(EventDetailsFields::start())
    ->limit(10)
    ->get();

Defaults: published posts only, all matching posts (no limit), the sort order of WordPress (newest first). The
statuses are taken as given, without checking the capabilities of the current user, like save().

content:
Attribute on parameters.

use Saij\WpAppFramework\Rest\Param;

Additional JSON schema keywords for a request argument of a #[RestRoute] method.

WordPress validates the keywords: minimum/maximum apply to int and float
parameters, minLength/maxLength/pattern/format to string parameters.

Arguments

#[Param(?string $description = null, int|float|null $minimum = null, int|float|null $maximum = null, ?int $minLength = null, ?int $maxLength = null, ?string $pattern = null, ?Format $format = null)]

Parameter	Type	Default	Description
description	string|null	null	Describes the argument in the schema, e.g. in the answer to an OPTIONS request; any parameter type.
minimum	int|float|null	null	The lowest allowed value, included; int and float parameters.
maximum	int|float|null	null	The highest allowed value, included; int and float parameters.
minLength	int|null	null	The minimum number of characters; string parameters.
maxLength	int|null	null	The maximum number of characters; string parameters.
pattern	string|null	null	A regular expression without delimiters that the value must match somewhere (anchor it with ^ and $ to match the whole value); string parameters. The build reports an invalid expression.
format	Format|null	null	A format WordPress validates or sanitizes the value with; string parameters.
description: Attribute on parameters. Additional JSON schema keywords for a request argument of a #[RestRoute] method. WordPress validates the keywords: minimum/maximum apply to int and float parameters, minLength/maxLength/pattern/format to string parameters.

title: Callback
content:
Class. It implements Permission.

use Saij\WpAppFramework\Rest\Permission\Callback;

A public static method decides, passed as first-class callable: new Callback(self::canEdit(...)).

The method returns bool. Its parameters follow the rules of the route method:
services are injected, WP_REST_Request receives the request, all other
parameters must be request arguments of the route with the same name and type.
It runs as permission_callback, after WordPress validated and sanitized the
arguments. Static, because PHP allows first-class callables in attribute
arguments only for static methods.

new Callback(Closure $callback)

callback	Closure	required	A first-class callable of a public static method that returns bool, e.g. self::canEdit(...).

Its parameters follow the rules of the route method: services are injected, WP_REST_Request receives the request, all other parameters must be request arguments of the route with the same name and type. It runs as permission_callback, after WordPress validated and sanitized the arguments. Static, because PHP allows first-class callables in attribute arguments only for static methods.

title: AbstractRow
content:
Abstract class.

use Saij\WpAppFramework\Table\AbstractRow;

The object of a row of a table of your own: a class with #[Table] extends it, and its promoted constructor
parameters are the columns.

A row object is loaded with LogEntry::get($id) or LogEntry::find($id), found with LogEntry::query() and
created with new LogEntry(…). save() inserts a new row and sets its primary key, or writes the changed columns of
a loaded one; a row object with a primary key whose row does not exist is inserted with that key. delete() deletes
it.

Every get(), find() and query returns new objects; when two of them change the same row, the last save() of a
column wins. save() and delete() check no capabilities.

Methods

find()

AbstractRow::find(int $id): ?static

The row with the primary key, null if it does not exist.

Parameter	Type	Default	Description
id	int	required	The primary key of the row.

Returns ?AbstractRow

get()

AbstractRow::get(int $id): static

The row with the primary key.

Parameter	Type	Default	Description
id	int	required	The primary key of the row.

Returns AbstractRow

Throws InvalidArgumentException: If it does not exist.

query()

AbstractRow::query(): RowQuery

A query for rows of the table: all rows in the order of their primary key, see RowQuery.

Returns RowQuery<AbstractRow>

tableName()

AbstractRow::tableName(): string

The full name of the table on the current site, for SQL of your own: {$wpdb->prefix}{namespace}_{name}.

Returns non-empty-string

delete()

delete(): void

Deletes the row; its primary key is null afterwards, so save() would insert it again.

Throws LogicException: If the row has not been saved yet.

save()

save(): void

Inserts the row and sets its primary key, or writes the columns changed since it was loaded or saved; without
changes, nothing is written. With a primary key whose row does not exist (set in new, or the row was deleted
in the meantime and the object changed since), the row is inserted with that primary key and all columns.

Throws RuntimeException: If the database refuses the row, e.g. a string longer than its column.
description: Abstract class. The object of a row of a table of your own: a class with #[Table] extends it, and its promoted constructor parameters are the columns. A row object is loaded with LogEntry::get($id) or LogEntry::find($id), found with LogEntry::query() and created with new LogEntry(…). save() inserts a new row and sets its primary key, or writes the changed columns of a loaded one; a row object with a primary key whose row does not exist is inserted with that key. delete() deletes it. Every get(), find() and query returns new objects; when two of them change the same row, the last save() of a column wins. save() and delete() check no capabilities.

title: RowQuery
content:
Class.

use Saij\WpAppFramework\Table\RowQuery;

A query for rows of a table, started with LogEntry::query() and returning row objects; it writes its SQL itself.

A query never changes: every method returns a changed copy, so a query can be passed on and varied safely. Keep
the result – $query->limit(3); alone does nothing, and PHP warns about it (#[\NoDiscard]).

$rows = LogEntry::query()
    ->where(LogEntryFields::level()->equals(Level::Error))
    ->orderBy(LogEntryFields::created(), Direction::Desc)
    ->limit(20)
    ->get();

Defaults: all rows, in the order of the primary key. Columns are compared as stored: strings without regard to
case (the collation of WordPress), NULL like PHP compares null – notEquals() and notIn() of a nullable column also
match rows without value. NULL sorts first in ascending order (MariaDB).

Methods

count()

count(): int

The number of all matching rows; limit() and offset() do not count.

Returns int

delete()

delete(): int

Deletes the matching rows (with limit(), the first ones in the order) and returns how many. Row objects loaded
before keep their primary key.

Returns int

Throws LogicException: With offset(): delete() cannot skip rows.

first()

first(): ?AbstractRow

The first matching row, null without one.

Returns T|null

get()

get(): array

The matching rows.

Returns list<T>

Throws LogicException: With offset() but without limit().

limit()

limit(int $limit): static

At most this many rows.

Parameter	Type	Default	Description
limit	int	required	The maximum number of rows, at least 1.

Returns RowQuery

Throws InvalidArgumentException: With a number below 1.

offset()

offset(int $offset): static

Skips this many rows (needs limit(); get() throws a LogicException without it, delete() with it).

Parameter	Type	Default	Description
offset	int	required	The number of rows to skip, at least 0.

Returns RowQuery

Throws InvalidArgumentException: With a negative number.

orderBy()

orderBy(Field $field, Direction $direction = Direction::Asc): static

Sorts by a column; further calls sort rows that are equal so far. Without orderBy(), rows come in the order of
their primary key.

Parameter	Type	Default	Description
field	Field	required	A field of this table, from its class with #[TableFields]; a field of another table throws an InvalidArgumentException.
direction	Direction	Direction::Asc	Ascending (default) or descending.

Returns RowQuery

where()

where(Condition ...$conditions): static

Rows that meet all conditions (columns, Any, All); adds to the conditions of earlier calls.

Parameter	Type	Default	Description
...conditions	Condition		Conditions created by the field classes of this table (a class with #[TableFields]), or groups of them with Any and All. Throws an InvalidArgumentException for conditions on meta fields or terms, or on a column of another table.

Returns RowQuery
description: Class. A query for rows of a table, started with LogEntry::query() and returning row objects; it writes its SQL itself. A query never changes: every method returns a changed copy, so a query can be passed on and varied safely. Keep the result – $query->limit(3); alone does nothing, and PHP warns about it (#[\NoDiscard]). Defaults: all rows, in the order of the primary key. Columns are compared as stored: strings without regard to case (the collation of WordPress), NULL like PHP compares null – notEquals() and notIn() of a nullable column also match rows without value. NULL sorts first in ascending order (MariaDB).

title: Theme
content:
Class.

use Saij\WpAppFramework\Theme;

Boots the framework for the active theme and provides its paths.

The instance is created only by boot() and handed to the container as a
predefined instance: the container never builds it, but services of a theme
can inject it to read the paths.

Methods

boot()

Theme::boot(): void

Boots the framework. Called once from the theme's functions.php.

Release mode applies if the theme contains generated/manifest.php (created
only by the release build). Otherwise development mode builds the manifest
by reflection and caches it in wp-content/cache/{template}/manifest.

title: #[TemplateFilter]
content:
Attribute on methods.

use Saij\WpAppFramework\Twig\TemplateFilter;

Registers a public method of a service as a Twig filter.

The filtered value is passed as the first parameter, filter arguments follow.
The service is resolved only when a template applies the filter. The return
value is escaped like any other output unless html is true; then it is
printed as is and the method must return a string. An HTML filter receives
the filtered value HTML-escaped unless it is already safe (e.g. |raw);
further arguments are passed unescaped and must be escaped by the method.

With public: true, a plugin offers the filter to the templates of other
consumers (the theme, other plugins), and a theme to the templates of its
child theme. Its name must start with the template prefix of the plugin or
theme (the slug with underscores, e.g. my_plugin_) and its signature must
not use classes of the framework or of other dependencies. Consumers declare
the plugin in extra.wp-app-framework.template-plugins of their
composer.json and call the filter by its name; for a child theme, its parent
theme is declared automatically. Child themes cannot offer filters.

Arguments

#[TemplateFilter(string $name, bool $html = false, bool $public = false)]

Parameter	Type	Default	Description
name	string	required	Name of the filter in templates, a valid identifier, e.g. highlight; it must not reuse a filter Twig provides.
html	bool	false	The method returns HTML (string), which is printed unescaped; it receives the filtered value HTML-escaped unless the value is already safe.
public	bool	false	Offer the filter to the templates of other consumers: a plugin to themes and other plugins, a theme to its child themes. The name must then start with the template prefix.
description: Attribute on methods. Registers a public method of a service as a Twig filter. The filtered value is passed as the first parameter, filter arguments follow. The service is resolved only when a template applies the filter. The return value is escaped like any other output unless html is true; then it is printed as is and the method must return a string. An HTML filter receives the filtered value HTML-escaped unless it is already safe (e.g. |raw); further arguments are passed unescaped and must be escaped by the method. With public: true, a plugin offers the filter to the templates of other consumers (the theme, other plugins), and a theme to the templates of its child theme. Its name must start with the template prefix of the plugin or theme (the slug with underscores, e.g. my_plugin_) and its signature must not use classes of the framework or of other dependencies. Consumers declare the plugin in extra.wp-app-framework.template-plugins of their composer.json and call the filter by its name; for a child theme, its parent theme is declared automatically. Child themes cannot offer filters.

title: TemplateRenderer
content:
Class.

use Saij\WpAppFramework\Twig\TemplateRenderer;

Renders the Twig templates of a framework instance (theme, child theme or plugin).

Template names are paths relative to the src/ directory of each level,
including the extension (e.g. Component/Button.twig). Names without a
namespace are looked up in the search paths of the instance, then in the
framework, so a higher level overrides a template by providing the same path:

theme: child theme overrides/{slug}/ → theme src/ → framework,

child theme: child theme src/ → framework,

plugin: child theme overrides/{slug}/ → theme overrides/{slug}/ → plugin src/ → framework.
@theme/… (themes, child themes), @plugin/… (plugins) and @framework/…
address exactly one level and cannot be overridden.

Names starting with the template prefix of a plugin declared in
extra.wp-app-framework.template-plugins, or in a child theme of its parent
theme, call the public template functions and filters of that plugin or theme.

Provided by the framework at runtime; services receive it through their
constructor. The Twig environment is created on the first render.

Constants

Constant	Value	Description
TEMPLATE_DIRECTORY	'src'	Directory of the templates inside each level, relative to its root.
OVERRIDE_DIRECTORY	'overrides'	Directory of a theme or child theme with overrides of templates of other instances, one subdirectory per slug.

Methods

render()

render(string $name, array $context = []): string

Renders a template.

Parameter	Type	Default	Description
name	string	required	E.g. Component/Button.twig or @framework/Component/Button.twig.
context	array<string, mixed>	[]	Template variables.

Returns string

Template names are paths relative to the src/ directory of each level, including the extension (e.g. Component/Button.twig). Names without a namespace are looked up in the search paths of the instance, then in the framework, so a higher level overrides a template by providing the same path: theme: child theme overrides/{slug}/ → theme src/ → framework,child theme: child theme src/ → framework,plugin: child theme overrides/{slug}/ → theme overrides/{slug}/ → plugin src/ → framework. @theme/… (themes, child themes), @plugin/… (plugins) and @framework/… address exactly one level and cannot be overridden. Names starting with the template prefix of a plugin declared in extra.wp-app-framework.template-plugins, or in a child theme of its parent theme, call the public template functions and filters of that plugin or theme. Provided by the framework at runtime; services receive it through their constructor. The Twig environment is created on the first render.

title: Link
content:
Class.

use Saij\WpAppFramework\Value\Link;

A link: a URL entered freely or a post, term or media file chosen in a
search, plus whether it opens in a new tab. Edited with the link control of
the block editor (a search form on the settings page and in classic meta
boxes); in blocks it counts as content. Never null: an empty URL means no
link. Templates print it with link_attributes().

A linked object is stored with its ID; when the value is created, the URL
becomes the current URL of the object, or empty if the object no longer
exists or is not public (renders for the block editor keep objects that are
not public, so editors see their choice). The stored URL of a linked object
is only what the editor showed when it was chosen.

Constructor

new Link(string $url = '', bool $opensInNewTab = false, LinkKind $kind = LinkKind::Url, int $id = 0)

Parameter	Type	Default	Description
url	string	''	The URL; for linked objects resolved when the value is created.
opensInNewTab	bool	false	Open the link in a new tab (target="_blank" rel="noopener").
kind	LinkKind	LinkKind::Url	A free URL or the kind of the linked object.
id	int	0	ID of the linked object; 0 for a free URL.
description: Class. A link: a URL entered freely or a post, term or media file chosen in a search, plus whether it opens in a new tab. title: ViewData
content:
Class.

use Saij\WpAppFramework\View\ViewData;

Data from PHP for the scripts of one framework instance: its views (of
blocks, block supports and the document), its editor scripts and its shared
modules read a value with this.data(key) or getData(key).

Inject it and set values before they are printed: on the front end the
framework prints them with the view runtime in the footer, so values from
hooks and from render() reach the views; in the editor it prints them with
the editor runtime at the end of enqueue_block_editor_assets. Setting a
value afterwards is an error. Every visitor can read the values.

#[Hook('wp')]
public function provideMap(ViewData $viewData): void
{
    $viewData->set('map', ['zoom' => 12]);
}

Methods

get()

get(string $key): mixed

The value set for the key.

Parameter	Type	Default	Description
key	string	required	The key the value was set with.

Returns mixed

Throws OutOfBoundsException: If no value is set for the key.

has()

has(string $key): bool

Whether a value is set for the key.

Parameter	Type	Default	Description
key	string	required	The key the value was set with.

Returns bool

set()

set(string $key, mixed $value): void

Sets a value; a later call with the same key replaces it.

Parameter	Type	Default	Description
key	string	required	Letters, digits, "-" and "_", starting with a letter.
value	mixed	required	null, a scalar or an array of these (no objects, no NAN or INF).

Throws InvalidArgumentException: If the key or the value is invalid.

Throws LogicException: If the values are already printed and WP_DEBUG is on.
description: Class. Data from PHP for the scripts of one framework instance: its views (of blocks, block supports and the document), its editor scripts and its shared modules read a value with this.data(key) or getData(key). Inject it and set values before they are printed: on the front end the framework prints them with the view runtime in the footer, so values from hooks and from render() reach the views; in the editor it prints them with the editor runtime at the end of enqueue_block_editor_assets. Setting a value afterwards is an error. Every visitor can read the values.

title: asset_image()
content:
Twig function of the framework; its result is HTML and is printed without escaping.

{{ asset_image(name, alt, attributes = {}) }}

An img element for an image asset with src, width and height (if known, so the page does not jump
while it loads), alt, decoding="async" and the given attributes. With widths and sizes the element
gets a srcset of smaller versions; with formats it is wrapped in a picture element with a source per
format. The build creates these variants from the calls in the templates, so the name, widths and formats
must be literals there. The output is HTML and is printed unescaped. An unknown or invalid name, or variants
the build did not create, are errors.

{{ asset_image('images/hero.jpg', 'Our team', {
    widths: [640, 1280, 1920],
    sizes: '(min-width: 1200px) 1200px, 100vw',
    formats: ['avif', 'webp'],
    class: 'w-full h-auto',
}) }}

Parameter	Type	Default	Description
name	string	required	Path of the asset below assets/, e.g. images/logo.svg; it may start with @child/ or with the instance's own prefix (@theme/ or @plugin/).
alt	string	required	The alternative text; '' for a decorative image.
attributes	array<string, string|int|bool|list<int>|list<string>>	[]	Further attributes; true adds one without value, false leaves it out. src, srcset and alt cannot be set. widths (list of pixel widths, needs sizes) and formats (avif, webp, jpeg, png) ask for variants.

Returns string

title: Webpack helper
content:
The webpack helper builds the editor runtime of your theme or plugin, your editor and view scripts, the shared modules and the stylesheet. Your webpack.config.js calls it:

module.exports = require( '@saij/wp-app-framework/webpack' )( {
	slug: 'my-theme',
	root: __dirname,
} );

Option	Meaning
slug	The slug of the theme or plugin: its directory name. The script handles and the JavaScript global derive from it.
root	The directory of the project.

Until 0.15 the helper was required by its path, ./vendor/saij/wp-app-framework/webpack.config.js; that still works.

Conventions

Source	Built to	Loaded
src/**/Name.editor.js next to a block or block support class	build/**/Name.editor.js	in the editor with the runtime
src/**/Name.view.js next to a block or block support class	build/**/Name.view.js	where the block renders
assets/**/*.editor.js	build/assets/**/*.editor.js	in the post and site editor
assets/**/*.view.js (document views)	build/assets/**/*.view.js	on every page of the front end
assets/shared/**/*.js, imported as #shared/<name>	build/assets/shared/**/*.js	with the scripts that import them
assets/styles.css	build/styles.css, build/styles.preload.php	on the front end and in the editor canvas

#shared/* needs the entry "imports": { "#shared/*": "./assets/shared/*.js" } in your package.json. The framework's own scripts go to build/vendor/wp-app-framework/. See Editor for the complete list, the script handles and the errors of the helper, and Front-end scripts and Styles.

Imports

Import	Resolves to
@saij/wp-app-framework	the editor API of your theme or plugin (see JavaScript); not in view scripts
@saij/wp-app-framework/view	the view API (see BlockView)
#shared/<name>	a shared module of your theme or plugin
@wordpress/*	the scripts of WordPress, as with @wordpress/scripts
description: The webpack helper builds the editor runtime of your theme or plugin, your editor and view scripts, the shared modules and the stylesheet. Your webpack.config.js calls it: Until 0.15 the helper was required by its path, ./vendor/saij/wp-app-framework/webpack.config.js; that still works.

title: Release workflow
content:
.github/workflows/consumer-release.yml of the framework releases a theme, child theme or plugin from a tag: it builds the ZIP, tests it in fresh WordPress instances and attaches it to the GitHub release. Call it from a workflow of your project:

on:
  push:
    tags: ['v*']

permissions:
  contents: write

jobs:
  release:
    uses: SaijSaij/wp-app-framework/.github/workflows/consumer-release.yml@v0.15.0
    with:
      cli: true

Input	Type	Default	Meaning
repository	string	the calling repository	the project to release
ref	string	the calling ref, i.e. the tag	the revision to build
e2e	boolean	true	run the browser tests (npm run test:e2e) against the release
e2e-instances	number	2	number of WordPress instances and Playwright workers for the browser tests
cli	boolean	false	run the WP-CLI tests tests/cli/run against the release
publish	boolean	true	attach the ZIP to the GitHub release of the tag; the tag must equal v and the version in the header
framework-ref	string	the locked version	build with another revision of the framework
wp-test-env-ref	string	main	the revision of wp-test-env that provides the tools and the WordPress instances
with-theme	string	–	required for plugins and child themes: the theme release as <owner>/<repository>@<tag>

See Releases and CI for what the workflow does step by step and what your tests receive.
description: .github/workflows/consumer-release.yml of the framework releases a theme, child theme or plugin from a tag: it builds the ZIP, tests it in fresh WordPress instances and attaches it to the GitHub release. Call it from a workflow of your project: See Releases and CI for what the workflow does step by step and what your tests receive.

title: Build
content:
The framework reads your attributes in a build step and turns them into a manifest (see Concepts). During development it runs that step itself on each request that needs it. You can also run it from the command line, which is useful in two situations:

To check your code. The build reports every problem it finds: a constructor parameter the container cannot fill, a REST route without permission, an invalid attribute, a typo in a block template. Running it before a commit or in CI catches mistakes without opening WordPress.

To write a release manifest. The release build uses it internally.

vendor/bin/wp-app-framework build [--output=<file>]

In a consumer created as in Getting started, composer build-manifest runs the same command.

Checking

Without --output, the command builds and checks the manifest and writes nothing. It builds the project whose vendor/autoload.php the Composer bin proxy loads, which is the project you run it in. Problems are listed with class and parameter names, and the exit code is 1.

If the build succeeds, the command prints what it found, for example:

Manifest OK (theme my-theme): 40 service candidates, 25 services, 3 hooks, 12 routes, 2 template functions, 1 template filters, 8 blocks, 4 CLI commands, 2 cron events, 1 cron tasks, 1 tables, 2 lifecycle methods. Nothing written (no --output).

The CLI commands are the subcommands of WP-CLI commands. Cron events and cron tasks are the recurring events and one-time tasks of Cron events and tasks, and tables are the row classes of Tables.

The command also lists the templates of the project that override templates of the framework, and the classes it did not load because they build on a class outside the project, such as a widget extending WP_Widget (see Classes that build on WordPress):

Not loaded by the build (building on a class outside the project, its Composer dependencies and PHP): MyTheme\Widget\NoteWidget (WP_Widget).

Checking templates, parts and patterns

A theme writes blocks into files as well: block templates in templates/, template parts in parts/ and patterns in patterns/. WordPress reads these files as they are. A misspelled attribute, a value the block does not know or HTML in a block that stores none would only show up when the page renders, or not at all, because WordPress drops what it cannot use without a word. The build therefore checks these files against the blocks of your theme.

Take a pattern with a card block whose attribute class has a title and a tone enum with the values light and dark:

<?php
/**
 * Title: Teaser
 * Slug: my-theme/teaser
 */
?>
<!-- wp:my-theme/card {"titel":"Welcome","tone":"pink"} /-->

The build stops with two errors, each with the file, the line and the block:

patterns/teaser.php:6: block my-theme/card: unknown attribute "titel".
patterns/teaser.php:6: block my-theme/card: attribute "tone": "pink" is not one of "light", "dark".

What is checked

The build reads every *.html below templates/ and parts/ and every *.php below patterns/, the files WordPress uses for a block theme. Each block of your theme is checked against its definition. The JSON in the block comment may only contain the attributes of the attribute class and of the block supports, each with a value that fits its schema: the right type, a value of the enum, the required properties of a value class and no others.

The block's structure is checked too. HTML between the block comments is only allowed in a block with a postContent field. Inner blocks are only allowed in a block whose render() takes $content, and only blocks it allows (#[InnerBlocks(allowed: …)]). A block with parent must sit directly in one of those blocks, a block with ancestor somewhere inside one. A container whose template is locked with TemplateLock::All or TemplateLock::ContentOnly must hold the blocks of its template, because the editor replaces differing inner blocks (see Container blocks).

Template parts and patterns with a single top-level block open in contentOnly mode in the editor (see Content in contentOnly mode). There, a block can only be inserted into a container that is itself a content block. A container of your theme without content that holds content blocks of your theme is therefore an error in such a template part or pattern; give it #[Supports(contentRole: true)].

Blocks of others

The build knows only the blocks of your own theme. Core blocks, blocks of plugins and, in a child theme, the blocks of the parent theme are not checked, because their definitions are not part of your build. Only their JSON must be valid.

A block name in the namespace of your theme (extra.wp-app-framework.namespace) must be one of your blocks: with the namespace my-theme, my-theme/crad is reported as an unknown block. Each theme and plugin has a namespace of its own, so the build can tell your blocks from those of others.

Plugins are not checked, because WordPress reads block templates, template parts and patterns from themes only. A child theme without code has no build, so nothing checks its files.

PHP in patterns

WordPress runs a pattern file as PHP and uses its output. The build cannot run it, so it reads the file as it is and skips the PHP code. PHP in the text of a block, such as a translated sentence in a core paragraph, is fine. PHP inside the block comment of one of your blocks is an error, because the attributes are then only known at run time. Write them as plain JSON.

Rules

The build reports these errors in block templates, template parts and patterns:

A block comment that WordPress would treat as HTML, such as <!--wp:my-theme/card /--> without a space.

A closing comment without an opening one, a closing comment for another block than the open one, and a block that is never closed. WordPress repairs these silently.

Invalid JSON in a block comment, for any block, unless the comment contains PHP. WordPress ignores all attributes of such a block.

An unknown block in the namespace of your own blocks.

In your own blocks:
an attribute that is neither in the attribute class, nor one of the block's supports, nor one of WordPress' attributes allowed by #[Supports] (lock and metadata always; className unless customClassName: false; anchor with anchor: true; align with one of the allowed alignments or ""; style unless customCSS: false);

a value with the wrong type, a value outside the enum, a missing required property or an unknown property of a value class;

the postContent field in the JSON instead of between the block comments;

HTML between the block comments without a postContent field;

inner blocks in a block without $content, and inner blocks missing from #[InnerBlocks(allowed: …)];

a block outside of the blocks in its parent or ancestor;

inner blocks of a container with a locked template (TemplateLock::All or ContentOnly) whose block names differ from the template;

PHP code in the block comment (patterns);

in a template part or a pattern with a single top-level block, a container that is not a content block but holds content blocks of your theme.


A directory block-templates/ or block-template-parts/. WordPress reads these deprecated directories instead of templates/ and parts/ as soon as one of them exists.

During development, the framework rebuilds the manifest when one of these files changes, so an error shows up on the next request.

Generating fields for queries

vendor/bin/wp-app-framework meta-fields <meta class> [--force]
vendor/bin/wp-app-framework table-fields <row class> [--force]

meta-fields writes the class with #[MetaFields] that queries use to filter and sort by the fields of a meta class: {MetaClass}Fields.php, next to the meta class. table-fields does the same for the columns of a row class: {RowClass}Fields.php with #[TableFields]. Neither replaces an existing file unless you pass --force. Unlike the build, the two write into your source code; the result is yours to change and commit.

Tables

The build checks the row classes of your tables – types, primary key, lengths, indexes, earlier names – and reports every declaration that the database could not create, with class and parameter; the rules list them. It also checks every class with #[TableFields] against its row class. The manifest gets the structure of the tables, a hash of it and the version from the Version: header of your theme or plugin.

Writing a manifest

With --output, the command writes the manifest to the given file. A written manifest is a release manifest and carries the template version, which names the directory of the release's Twig cache.

Do not write generated/manifest.php into a source checkout of a theme or plugin. Its presence switches the project to release mode (see Boot and modes), and the framework stops noticing changes to your code. The release build writes it into its own copy of the project.

title: Releases and CI
content:
Releasing a theme or plugin should be a single step: push a tag. The framework provides a GitHub Actions workflow that does the rest. It builds the release ZIP, installs it into a plain WordPress, runs your browser tests against it, and attaches the ZIP to the GitHub release only if everything passed. A ZIP that fails its tests is never published.

Tags follow semantic versioning with a v prefix: v1.2.0.

Themes, child themes and plugins

Your repository calls the reusable workflow .github/workflows/consumer-release.yml of the framework repository from a workflow of its own. That workflow runs on push: tags: ['v*'] and needs permissions: contents: write to attach the ZIP. The test projects theme-dev-test, theme-dev-test-child and plugin-dev-test contain working examples to copy.

Pin the workflow to a framework tag, so a new framework version never changes your release process unannounced.

The workflow:

checks out the project and wp-test-env, the test environment it runs in;

runs composer lint and npm run lint, if they are defined, and wp-app-framework build;

builds the release; when it publishes, with --expect-version set to the version of the tag, so a tag that doesn't match Version: fails;

installs the ZIP into fresh, plain WordPress instances of wp-test-env, with the plugin and theme directories read-only;

with the input cli: true, runs the project's WP-CLI tests against the installed release (see below);

runs the project's browser tests (npm run test:e2e) with E2E_TARGET=release, one Playwright worker per instance (input e2e-instances, default 2); the input e2e: false skips them.

Plugins and child themes need a theme

A theme can be tested on its own, but a plugin or a child theme needs a theme to run in. The workflow decides from the type in composer.json and the Template: header of style.css:

a plugin is installed next to the release ZIP of a theme;

a child theme is installed on top of the release ZIP of its parent theme.

The input with-theme: <owner>/<repository>@<tag> names that theme release. It is required for plugins and child themes.

WP-CLI tests

Browser tests can't run WP-CLI commands. With cli: true, the workflow runs the executable tests/cli/run of your project after the release is installed. Its only argument is the name of the wp-test-env instance with the release; wp-test-env is checked out next to your project. The script runs your commands with ../wp-test-env/bin/wp "$1" … (relative to your project) and fails with a non-zero exit code if an output or exit code is not what you expect. During development, run the same script against an instance of wp-test-env in development mode.

Browser tests

The workflow runs the browser tests with bin/e2e of wp-test-env: npm run test:e2e of your project in the Playwright image of its @playwright/test version. Every instance gets its own Playwright worker, so tests of different workers never share a site. Your Playwright configuration receives the instance URLs in WP_BASE_URLS (comma-separated), the administrator in WP_USERNAME and WP_PASSWORD, E2E_TARGET and a writable results directory in E2E_OUTPUT_DIR; it sets workers to the number of URLs and lets each worker pick its URL by TEST_PARALLEL_INDEX. The README of wp-test-env explains the contract; the configurations of the test projects are working examples.

Inputs

Input	Default	Purpose
repository	the calling repository	the project to release
ref	the calling ref, i.e. the tag	the revision to build
e2e	true	run the browser tests (npm run test:e2e) against the release
cli	false	run the WP-CLI tests tests/cli/run against the release
publish	true	attach the ZIP to the GitHub release of the tag
framework-ref	the locked version	build with another revision of the framework (the framework's release gate uses it)
e2e-instances	2	number of WordPress instances and Playwright workers for the browser tests
wp-test-env-ref	main	the revision of wp-test-env that provides the tools and the WordPress instances
with-theme	–	the theme release for plugins and child themes, <owner>/<repository>@<tag>

The framework

The framework repository tests itself in two workflows:

ci.yml runs PHPUnit, Vitest and all linters on pushes and pull requests, and builds this documentation.

release.yml runs on a tag. It runs the same checks and then the release gates: theme-dev-test, plugin-dev-test and theme-dev-test-child are built with the framework of the tag (framework-ref) and tested in the browser, the plugin and the child theme with an older release of the theme, without publishing anything. Only then does it attach wp-app-framework-<version>.zip to the GitHub release – made with git archive, without the development files marked export-ignore – and publish the documentation of the tag's minor version.

The gates make sure that a framework release works for a theme, a plugin and a child theme before anyone can depend on it.

Requiring the framework

The framework is on Packagist. Packagist reads the tags of the GitHub repository and updates itself on every push, so a release can be required as soon as its tag exists. Themes and plugins require a version range, and the lock file pins the exact version:

"require": {"saij/wp-app-framework": "^0.15"}

The test projects of the framework require dev-main instead, so they always build with the latest framework.

toc.text: Plugins and child themes need a theme

description: Releasing a theme or plugin should be a single step: push a tag. The framework provides a GitHub Actions workflow that does the rest. It builds the release ZIP, installs it into a plain WordPress, runs your browser tests against it, and attaches the ZIP to the GitHub release only if everything passed. A ZIP that fails its tests is never published. Tags follow semantic versioning with a v prefix: v1.2.0.

title: Release
content:
A framework theme or plugin cannot simply be zipped from its Git checkout. The checkout has no vendor/, the editor scripts are not built, and the dependencies are not prefixed. A site with two framework consumers would load one framework for both of them.

wp-app-framework release turns a checkout into a ZIP that runs in any plain WordPress installation, without Composer on the server. It ships all dependencies, including the framework and Twig, prefixed with the project's own namespace in vendor-prefixed/. Several consumers with different framework versions can therefore run side by side.

vendor/bin/wp-app-framework release [--output=<zip>] [--expect-version=<version>] [--package-source=<package>=<directory>]...

In a consumer created as in Getting started, composer release runs the same command. It recognizes a theme or a plugin by the type in its composer.json.

What the release build does

The command works on a copy in the system's temporary directory and never changes your checkout. It runs these steps:

Copy the project. It copies the files Git does not ignore (git ls-files --cached --others --exclude-standard), so uncommitted changes are included. generated/manifest.php must not exist in the checkout.

Install the dependencies. It runs composer install --no-dev --classmap-authoritative from the lock file, so the release contains exactly the versions you tested.

Prefix the dependencies. Strauss renames every dependency into the project's namespace and rewrites the project's own code to use the new names. Strauss must be in the PATH (the tools images of wp-dev-env and wp-test-env provide it); the release command runs it with PHP and a memory limit of 512 MB, since it parses the large class map of the dependencies.
Then the command patches Twig. Twig's compiler writes class names such as use Twig\Environment; as plain strings into every compiled template, and no prefixing tool rewrites strings. Release\TwigPatcher rewrites exactly these places. It expects each pattern a fixed number of times, so a Twig update that changes them fails the build instead of producing a broken release.

Build the manifest. It builds generated/manifest.php with the prefixed classes (using bin/wp-app-framework-prefixed.php in the prefixed copy) and writes the template version into it, and the image variants the templates ask for into generated/assets/ (with Imagick or GD of the PHP that runs the release). Then it compiles all templates of the project and the framework, as release mode would, and checks the compiled code for names that were not prefixed.

Build the assets. If there is a package.json, it runs npm ci && npm run build, which also builds the editor runtime from vendor/. Then it checks that every built file the framework loads at run time exists, because a missing one would only fail on the page that needs it. The manifest decides which files these are:
The project has	It needs in build/
blocks, post meta or editor scripts in assets/	vendor/wp-app-framework/editor.asset.php (editor runtime)
blocks	vendor/wp-app-framework/canvas.asset.php (canvas styles)
an editor or view script of a block or block support	that script's .asset.php
a document view, an editor script or a shared module in assets/	that script's .asset.php below assets/
view scripts or document views	vendor/wp-app-framework/view.asset.php (view runtime)
settings groups	vendor/wp-app-framework/settings.asset.php (settings page)
post meta	vendor/wp-app-framework/meta-box.asset.php (meta boxes)
assets/styles.css	styles.css
fonts marked for preloading in assets/styles.css	styles.preload.php
Static assets in assets/ and the image variants in generated/assets/ are checked as well. A missing file stops the release with a list of the missing files and what needs them. A project without blocks, post meta, settings and stylesheet needs no package.json; one with them needs a package.json with a build script and a webpack.config.js with the framework's webpack helper.

Remove development files. It removes node_modules/, vendor/, composer.json, composer.lock, package.json, package-lock.json and every path the project marks export-ignore in .gitattributes (use dir/** for directories). Then it checks all PHP files for names of dependencies that were not prefixed, in string literals too. Inside vendor-prefixed/ string literals are not checked, because dependencies mention their own class names in messages.

Write the ZIP. It writes dist/<slug>-<version>.zip, or the file given with --output, with the project directory as root. The slug is the directory name. The version is the Version: header of the theme's or child theme's style.css, or of the plugin's main file <slug>.php. --expect-version makes the build fail if the version differs, which CI uses to compare it with the tag.

A child theme is built without its parent theme. Calls of the parent's public template callables compile without it.

Every step fails with the file, command or setting at fault. On failure the build directory is kept, and its path is printed, so you can look at what went wrong.

Strauss settings

The project declares the Strauss settings in its composer.json. The command cannot add them itself, because extra is part of the lock file's content hash. It checks the values it relies on instead:

"extra": {
    "strauss": {
        "target_directory": "vendor-prefixed",
        "namespace_prefix": "Vendor\\Theme\\Vendor\\",
        "classmap_prefix": "Vendor_Theme_Vendor_",
        "include_root_autoload": true,
        "update_call_sites": ["src", "functions.php"],
        "delete_vendor_packages": false
    }
}

namespace_prefix and classmap_prefix name the prefix for the dependencies. The prefix must not be the project's own namespace, which is Strauss' default.

update_call_sites lists where Strauss rewrites your code to the prefixed names. It must contain the file that boots the framework: functions.php of a theme or child theme, <slug>.php of a plugin.

Leave constant_prefix unset. It would rename the constants that the Symfony polyfills define for PHP itself, such as MB_CASE_UPPER. Twig defines no constants.

Unreleased framework changes

Normally the release uses the framework version from the lock file. To test a release with framework changes that are not released yet, replace the package with a local checkout:

composer release -- --package-source=saij/wp-app-framework=../wp-app-framework

--package-source=<package>=<directory> copies the checkout's files without those marked export-ignore, like a distribution archive. The output says that the build is not from the lock file. Composer path repositories are not supported, because the temporary copy has no sibling checkouts.

Distribution

The release ZIP is what you hand on – the source checkout never goes to a site. Where it goes depends on what you built.

A plugin that others may use belongs in the plugin directory of WordPress.org. You commit the content of the release ZIP to the plugin's SVN repository. The directory requires every file of a plugin to be under a license compatible with the GPL; the framework, Twig and the release build meet that, as long as your own code does too. Sites built with Bedrock then install the plugin with Composer from a mirror of the directory, such as repo.wp-packages.org, like any other plugin from WordPress.org.

A theme built with the framework cannot go into the theme directory of WordPress.org. Its review requirements forbid custom blocks and custom post types in themes, and blocks are what a framework theme is made of. A theme built for one site therefore lives in that site's repository – in a Bedrock site under web/app/themes/<slug> – and the deployment builds its release there:

cd web/app/themes/my-theme && composer release

The release command works in a subdirectory of another repository: it collects the files of the theme's directory with Git. The deployment then puts the content of the ZIP in place of the theme's source directory. The same applies to a plugin that only one site uses.

Rules:

The release ZIP contains the directory <slug>/ with everything the theme or plugin needs; nothing is installed on the server.

The framework and its dependencies are licensed under the GPL-2.0-or-later; a theme or plugin that ships them must be GPL-compatible as well.

Never deploy the source checkout: it runs in development mode, with unprefixed classes and without the release build's checks.
