title: Activation, deactivation and uninstallation
content:
A plugin or theme leaves traces in WordPress: cron events, options, tables, posts. Some work belongs to the moments when it starts and stops: a plugin creates a default page when it is activated, pauses a connection to a service when it is deactivated, and removes everything it stored when it is deleted. Without help, every plugin repeats the same code: activation and deactivation hooks, an uninstall.php that needs to know the names of every option and table, a loop over the sites of a network.

The framework does the part that follows from your declarations by itself. It removes the cron events of a deactivated plugin or a theme the site switched away from, and when a plugin is deleted, it removes the data the plugin declared. For everything else you mark methods with #[OnActivation], #[OnDeactivation] and #[OnUninstall].

When WordPress activates and deactivates

Plugins and themes start and stop in different ways.

A plugin is activated and deactivated on the plugins screen or with wp plugin activate and wp plugin deactivate. WordPress fires an action for this in the same request. A plugin is deleted only while it is inactive; WordPress then runs its uninstallation and removes its files.

A theme is never activated on its own: the site switches from one theme to another. WordPress fires switch_theme in the request that switches, while the old theme is still loaded, and after_switch_theme on the next request, with the new theme. The framework treats the first as the deactivation of the old theme and the second as the activation of the new one. A theme and its own child theme count as one: switching from a theme to its child theme, or back, neither deactivates nor activates the parent theme, because it stays loaded. A child theme with code of its own is an instance of its own (see Child themes): switching from the parent theme to it activates it, switching back deactivates it.

Themes cannot be uninstalled. WordPress loads no code of a theme it deletes, so nothing can clean up after a theme. This is often what you want: when someone switches back to the theme, its settings and tables are still there.

What the framework does by itself

Moment	Plugin	Theme and child theme
Activation	The rewrite rules are flushed on the next request. Cron events are scheduled on the next request, tables are created on the next request or the first access.	The same.
Deactivation	All cron events and tasks of the plugin are removed.	All cron events and tasks of the theme are removed.
Uninstallation	All data of the plugin is removed (see below).	–

Methods of your own

A lifecycle method is a public method of a service that returns void. Its parameters are services; WordPress passes nothing the method could use. Take a plugin that keeps a page with its overview:

use Saij\WpAppFramework\Lifecycle\OnActivation;

final readonly class OverviewPage
{
    public function __construct(private PageStore $pages) {}

    #[OnActivation]
    public function create(): void
    {
        $this->pages->ensureOverview();
    }
}

When the plugin is activated, create() runs. The methods of the plugin's post types and tables work already: the framework registers the post types of the plugin first, and a table is created on its first access.

#[OnDeactivation] works the same way. It runs before the framework removes the cron events, so the method can still look at them:

#[OnDeactivation]
public function pause(SyncClient $client): void
{
    $client->unsubscribe();
}

#[OnUninstall] runs when the plugin is deleted, before the framework removes its data. Use it for what the framework does not know about, such as an option you write with update_option() yourself or a file in the uploads directory:

#[OnUninstall]
public function removeExports(ExportDirectory $exports): void
{
    $exports->deleteAll();
}

A class may have any number of lifecycle methods, and one method may have several of the attributes. The methods of one moment run in the order of their class and method names.

If a method throws, the framework rethrows the exception when WP_DEBUG is on. Activating a plugin then fails with the error, as WordPress shows it for any plugin. Without WP_DEBUG, the error is logged and the next method runs, like a failing hook.

What the uninstallation removes

When a plugin is deleted, the framework first runs the #[OnUninstall] methods, then removes on each site:

every post of the plugin's post types, in any status, with its meta, comments and revisions,

every term of the plugin's taxonomies,

the meta keys of its meta classes, also from posts of other types, such as Post and Page,

the options of its settings groups,

its cron events and tasks,

its tables, with the tables an earlier namespace of the plugin left, and the state of their sync,

its technical options: the versions of cache tags, cache entries stored as transients, the rewrite hash, notices of the meta box.

Then it deletes the plugin's cache directory wp-content/cache/{slug} and lets WordPress rebuild its rewrite rules, which still contain the plugin's post types.

The framework removes only names it knows exactly: names from the build, or options in the exact form it writes them. It never deletes "everything that starts with the plugin's prefix", because another plugin whose namespace starts the same way (shop and shop-extras) would lose its data.

Some things stay:

Attachments uploaded to the deleted posts. They stay in the media library; WordPress does not delete them with a post.

Blocks of the plugin in other posts. They render nothing without the plugin.

Entries of a persistent object cache. They are never read again, because the versions of their tags are gone, and expire with their lifetime.

Everything the plugin stored without the framework: options, user meta, files. Remove it in an #[OnUninstall] method.

WordPress runs an uninstall.php of a plugin instead of the uninstall hook the framework registers. A plugin with this file would keep all its data, so the file is a build error. Move its code into a method with #[OnUninstall].

WordPress needs a static callback for the uninstall hook and stores it in the option uninstall_plugins. The framework registers it when the plugin is activated and again when it is deactivated, since a plugin is always deactivated before it is deleted. When WordPress uninstalls the plugin, it loads the plugin's main file first, so the plugin boots; this happens after init, and the framework registers the plugin's post types and taxonomies itself before the uninstallation runs.

Multisite

Every site of a network has its own options, cron events and tables. The framework therefore runs everything site by site:

Activating a plugin network-wide activates it on every site of the network; deactivating it network-wide deactivates it on every site. The lifecycle methods run once per site, with that site as the current one.

A site created while the plugin is active network-wide is activated as soon as WordPress has set it up.

Deleting a site drops the tables of the plugin on that site, together with the tables of WordPress.

Deleting the plugin uninstalls it on every site of every network.

On a large network, activating, deactivating and deleting a plugin takes a while, since each site is handled in turn.

Rules

Attribute	Runs	Allowed in
#[OnActivation]	Plugin: when it is activated (activate_{plugin}), per site when network-wide, and for new sites of a network where it is active network-wide. Theme: on the first request after the switch to it (after_switch_theme), unless the previous theme was the theme itself or its child theme.	Plugins, themes, child themes
#[OnDeactivation]	Plugin: when it is deactivated (deactivate_{plugin}), per site when network-wide. Theme: in the request that switches away from it (switch_theme), unless the new theme is the theme itself or its child theme.	Plugins, themes, child themes
#[OnUninstall]	When the plugin is deleted, on every site, before the framework removes its data.	Plugins only

Build errors:

The method is not public, is static or does not return void.

A parameter is not a service, or is variadic or passed by reference.

The class is not a service (for example #[NoService]).

#[OnUninstall] in a theme or child theme.

A plugin has an uninstall.php. In development mode, the boot reports the file as well, since the cached manifest does not notice a new file.

title: Plugins
description: A plugin uses the framework just like a theme. It boots its own instance with Plugin::boot(__FILE__) (see Boot and modes) and has its own blocks, hooks, REST routes, templates and settings. Everything in the guides applies to plugins as well. What is special about plugins is that they often work together with a theme. A plugin may provide data the theme displays, or helpers the theme's templates call. This page explains how a plugin – or a theme, towards its child theme – offers such an interface, and how the theme changes the plugin's markup.

title: Posts
description: Many sites need content of their own kind besides posts and pages: events, team members, venues, products. WordPress calls these post types, and their extra values post meta. Registering them by hand means a long list of arguments for register_post_type(), a meta key per value with a schema for the REST API, a form in the editor and code that reads the stored strings back into typed values. The framework lets you declare all of this with classes, as you do with blocks and settings: a post class declares a post type and is at the same time the object of a post of that type: you load, change and save posts through it;a meta class declares typed fields that belong to posts of one or more post types;a taxonomy class declares a taxonomy for post types. The build checks the declarations, and the framework registers everything on init, adds the forms to the editor and keeps the URLs working.

title: Queries
content:
A page often shows a list of posts: the next five events, the events of a genre, a page of news. In plain WordPress you describe such a list as an array of arguments for WP_Query, with the names of post types, meta keys and taxonomies as strings. A typo finds nothing, and your editor cannot help you. The framework lets you write the same query with the classes you already have. You start at the post class, add conditions on meta fields and terms, sort, and get post objects back: $events = Event::query() ->where(EventDetailsFields::capacity()->greaterThan(10)) ->where(Terms::in(Genre::class, [$jazz])) ->orderBy(EventDetailsFields::start()) ->limit(5) ->get(); Every name in this query is a class or a method, so your editor completes it and PHPStan checks it. The framework turns the query into arguments of WP_Query and runs it there. Plugins that filter queries, for example translation plugins, keep working. How it works Event::query() returns a PostQuery for posts of the type. A query never changes: every method returns a changed copy. You can therefore keep a query, pass it to other code and vary it without side effects: $upcoming = Event::query()->where(EventDetailsFields::start()->greaterOrEqual($today)); $teaser = $upcoming->limit(3)->get(); $total = $upcoming->count(); // counts all upcoming events, not 3 The flip side is that a call whose result you do not keep does nothing. To make that mistake visible, every method that returns a query carries PHP's #[\NoDiscard]. PHP warns when you drop the result, and PHPStan reports the line: $query->limit(3); // warning: the result is discarded $query = $query->limit(3); // right Without further methods, a query finds all published posts of the type, sorted the way WordPress sorts them (newest first). The methods get(), first(), count() and paginate() run the query. Meta fields in queries To filter or sort by a meta field, the query needs the field as an object. A field object knows its meta class, its name and its type. The type decides which comparisons it offers: an IntField takes integers, an EnumField takes the cases of EventKind. The field objects come from a class of their own next to the meta class, marked with #[MetaFields]. This keeps the meta class as it is, and you decide for each meta class whether its fields can be queried at all. Generating the class The quickest way is to let the framework write it. Run this in your theme or plugin: vendor/bin/wp-app-framework meta-fields 'Sections\Post\EventDetails' The command writes EventDetailsFields.php into the directory of EventDetails, with one method per field that can be queried: #[MetaFields(EventDetails::class)] final class EventDetailsFields { public static function capacity(): IntField { return new IntField(EventDetails::class, 'capacity'); } /** * @return EnumField */ public static function kind(): EnumField { return new EnumField(EventDetails::class, 'kind', EventKind::class); } /** * @return PostField */ public static function venue(): PostField { return new PostField(EventDetails::class, 'venue', Venue::class); } } The file is ordinary source code of your project. Commit it, remove methods you do not need, or add a method later. The command does not replace an existing file unless you pass --force. Together with table-fields for tables, it is the only command of the framework that writes source code, and it does so only when you run it. Writing it by hand You can also write the class yourself, for example with just the one field you query. The build checks it either way: it calls every public static method that returns a field and reports a field of another meta class, a field name that does not exist, a field class that does not fit the type, and a field that cannot be queried. Fields that hold a list or a value class cannot be queried. WordPress stores them serialized in one meta value, and SQL cannot look inside. Missing values A post that was never saved with a field has no meta value for it. When you load the meta object, such a field has the default of its constructor parameter. Queries follow the same rule. If the default meets a condition, the condition also finds posts without a stored value: capacity()->lessThan(5) finds events without a stored capacity, because the default is 0. Sorting follows it too: a post without a value sorts like the default. WordPress' own sorting by meta values cannot do this reliably, so the framework adds the sort order to the SQL of the query itself. It uses a filter of WordPress that it adds only while the query runs. Conditions where() takes conditions; all of them must be met. Conditions come from field objects, from Terms for taxonomies, and from the groups Any and All: $events = Event::query() ->where( Any::of( EventDetailsFields::kind()->equals(EventKind::Jazz), EventDetailsFields::venue()->equals($venue), ), Terms::notIn(Genre::class, [$children]), ) ->get(); Any::of() is met if one of its conditions is met, All::of() if all of them are; groups can contain groups. WordPress keeps conditions on meta fields and on terms in two separate parts of a query and always joins the two with AND. A group therefore contains either meta conditions or term conditions; mixing them throws an exception. The same field classes and groups work for the columns of tables of your own, in LogEntry::query(). A query of posts takes no conditions on columns, and a query of rows none on meta fields or terms. The data of the post has methods of its own, described in the next section. Posts and pages Queries work the same for the post types of WordPress: Post::query() returns posts, Page::query() pages. The fields every post has – slug, title, dates, parent, template, format, password, comments – have methods of their own, because they are columns of the posts table or data WordPress keeps in a fixed place, not fields of a meta class: $news = Post::query() ->where(Terms::in(Category::class, [$news]), Terms::notIn(Tag::class, [$internal])) ->format(PostFormat::Standard, PostFormat::Video) ->sticky(false) ->modifiedAfter(new DateTimeImmutable('-7 days')) ->search('concert', columns: [SearchColumn::Title]) ->get(); $imprint = Page::query()->slug('imprint')->first(); $wide = Page::query()->parentIn($about, $team)->template('page-wide')->orderBy(PostOrder::MenuOrder)->get(); WordPress' categories and tags are named by the framework classes Category and Tag, like its post types by Post and Page. They register nothing and work wherever a taxonomy class is accepted: in Terms, getTerms(), TaxonomyTag and #[TermReference]. A few fields need a word of explanation: Template: WordPress stores the template of a post in the protected meta key _wp_page_template, as the slug of the file in templates/. template('page-wide') finds posts with that template, defaultTemplate() posts without one. Format: post formats are terms of the taxonomy post_format. Since you know them as a fixed list, format() takes the enum PostFormat; PostFormat::Standard is a post without format. Sticky: WordPress keeps the IDs of sticky posts in the option sticky_posts. sticky() reads it when the query runs, so a cached query notices a change. Only posts of the type post can be sticky. Search: without further arguments, search() looks in the title, excerpt and content, like the search of WordPress. columns limits it, exact requires the text to be the whole value of a column, and sentence searches the words as one phrase. Sorting and pages orderBy() sorts by post data (PostOrder::Title, PostOrder::Date, …) or a field, ascending unless you pass Direction::Desc. Each further call sorts the posts that are still equal. limit() and offset() restrict get(). For pages, use paginate(), which also counts all matching posts: $page = Event::query()->orderBy(PostOrder::Date, Direction::Desc)->paginate(perPage: 10, page: $number); foreach ($page->getPosts() as $event) { /* … */ } $pages = $page->getPageCount(); Caching cache() stores the result in the cache of your theme or plugin. The framework stores the IDs of the posts and the number of matching posts, and loads the post objects from them on each call: $events = Event::query()->where(Terms::in(Genre::class, [$jazz]))->cache(ttl: 600)->get(); You do not need to name tags for the posts. The framework adds the tag of the post type and of every taxonomy in the conditions, so a changed event, meta value or term assignment invalidates the entry. Further tags and variants work as with remember(). A random order cannot be cached. WordPress caches the IDs of queries in the object cache as well, but only with a persistent object cache, and every change of any post invalidates all of them. cache() also works with the file backend and is invalidated per post type. Using results in templates Queries belong in PHP, not in templates. A block runs its query in render() and passes the post objects to its template, where their getters work as with post(): public function render(EventListAttributes $attrs): string { return $this->renderer->render('Block/EventList/EventList.twig', [ 'events' => Event::query()->limit($attrs->limit)->get(), ]); } {% for event in events %} {{ event.title }} {% endfor %} Rules AbstractPost::query() returns a PostQuery of the post class; it works once the theme or plugin has booted. Every method that returns a query is marked #[\NoDiscard]. Method Effect where(Condition ...$conditions) All conditions must be met; adds to earlier calls. status(PostStatus ...) These statuses instead of Publish. The capabilities of the current user are not checked. ids(AbstractPost|int ...) Only these posts; without arguments no posts at all. exclude(AbstractPost|int ...) Not these posts; adds to earlier calls. Next to ids() the posts are taken out of the IDs, because WordPress ignores its own exclusion when IDs are given. author(int ...) Posts of these authors. parent(AbstractPost|int|null) Children of the post (an object or its ID), or top-level posts with null; hierarchical post types only. search(string, list $columns = [], bool $exact = false, bool $sentence = false) The search of WordPress; the text must not be empty. Without columns: title, excerpt and content. slug(string ...) Posts with one of the slugs (post_name). title(string) Posts with exactly this title. parentIn(AbstractPost|int ...), parentNotIn(…) Children of one of the posts, or no children of them; hierarchical post types only. modifiedAfter(DateTimeInterface), modifiedBefore(…) Date of the last change, the time itself excluded. template(string ...), defaultTemplate() Posts with one of the templates (slug), or without template. format(PostFormat ...) Posts with one of the formats; Standard is a post without format. sticky(bool = true) Sticky posts only, or no sticky posts; Post::query() only. hasPassword(bool = true) Posts with a password, or without one. menuOrder(int) Posts with this menu order (at least 0). commentCount(int, Comparison = Equal) Posts whose number of approved comments compares to the number. commentStatus(DiscussionStatus), pingStatus(DiscussionStatus) Posts whose comments or pings are open or closed. publishedAfter(DateTimeInterface), publishedBefore(…) Publication date, the time itself excluded. orderBy(PostOrder|Field, Direction = Asc) Sorts; further calls sort what is still equal. Without it: newest first. limit(int), offset(int) At most this many posts (at least 1), skipping some (with limit()). Without limit(), all posts. cache(int $ttl, array $tags = [], array $vary = []) Caches the result; tags of the post type and the taxonomies are added. get() The posts, as objects of the post class. first() The first post or null. count() The number of all matching posts, regardless of limit() and offset(). paginate(int $perPage, int $page) A PostPage with getPosts(), getTotal(), getPage(), getPerPage() and getPageCount(); not with limit() or offset(). A value outside the allowed range, such as limit(0), throws an InvalidArgumentException when you call the method. A combination that does not fit, such as offset() without limit() or paginate() after limit(), throws a LogicException when the query runs. Fields and their conditions: Field of the meta class Field class Conditions string (also #[PlainText], #[RichText], #[Url]) StringField equals, notEquals, in, notIn, greaterThan, greaterOrEqual, lessThan, lessOrEqual, between, contains int IntField as StringField, without contains float FloatField as IntField bool BoolField equals backed enum EnumField equals, notEquals, in, notIn post class (?Venue) PostField

equals, in, notIn, isNull, isNotNull #[Image], #[PostReference], #[TermReference], #[UserReference] on ?int IdField equals, in, notIn, isNull, isNotNull Strings are compared without regard to case, like the default collations of the database. contains() matches % and _ literally. A meta value that is not stored counts as the default in conditions and in the sort order. Terms::in(), notIn() and all() take the taxonomy class, a non-empty list of WP_Term objects or term IDs and includeChildren (default true); Terms::exists() and notExists() take the taxonomy class. Any::of() and All::of() need at least one condition, all on meta fields, all on terms or all on the columns of a table. DateTimeField and the Nullable… field classes are for tables only. #[MetaFields(metaClass)] on a class of your own: metaClass is a meta class (#[PostMeta]) of the theme or plugin; one class per meta class. Every public static method that returns a field has no parameters and returns a field of metaClass with an existing field name and the field class of its type (with the enum or post class of the field). Other methods are ignored. The class is no service. In development mode the build runs again when signatures change, not when only a method body changes; a query checks its fields again when it runs. wp-app-framework meta-fields [--force] writes {MetaClass}Fields.php next to the meta class. An existing file is replaced only with --force.

title: REST routes
content:
A REST route in WordPress needs more code than it seems. You call register_rest_route(), write an args schema for validation, add a permission callback, read and convert the parameters, and turn errors into WP_Error objects with the right status code. Forgetting the permission callback makes the route public.

With the framework, a route is a method with #[RestRoute]. The framework derives the argument schema from the method signature, so WordPress validates and sanitizes the arguments before your code runs. The permission is a required argument of the attribute, so your IDE and the build report a route without one.

Controller and routes

Routes live in a controller class. #[RestController] on the class sets the REST namespace and an optional base path for all its routes:

use Saij\WpAppFramework\Rest\HttpMethod;
use Saij\WpAppFramework\Rest\Permission\PublicAccess;
use Saij\WpAppFramework\Rest\RestController;
use Saij\WpAppFramework\Rest\RestException;
use Saij\WpAppFramework\Rest\RestRoute;

#[RestController('v1', base: '/items')]
final class ItemController
{
    #[RestRoute('/{id}', HttpMethod::Get, new PublicAccess())]
    public function show(int $id, ItemRepository $items, Variant $variant = Variant::Short): array
    {
        return $items->find($id) ?? throw new RestException('sections_item_not_found', 'Item not found.', 404);
    }
}

With the namespace sections (extra.wp-app-framework.namespace in composer.json), this registers GET /wp-json/sections/v1/items/{id}. Read the method signature from left to right:

int $id matches the placeholder {id} in the path. Because it is an int, the route only matches digits.

ItemRepository $items is a service, so the framework injects it.

Variant $variant = Variant::Short is a backed enum with a default, so it becomes an optional request argument (?variant=long). WordPress accepts only the enum's values, and the method receives the enum case.

The method returns an array, which becomes a JSON response with status 200. If the item does not exist, it throws a RestException with status 404.

#[RestController(version, base: '')] takes the version without leading or trailing slash, for example v1; the value may be a class constant. The routes are registered under {namespace}/{version}, where the namespace is the one of your theme or plugin (see Concepts). A #[RestRoute] in a class without #[RestController] is a build error.

#[RestRoute(path, methods, permission)] is repeatable, and all three arguments are required, so the IDE and the build both report a missing permission. path is empty or starts with /. methods is an HttpMethod case or a list of them.

Permission

Every route says who may call it. There are three kinds of permission, all in the namespace Saij\WpAppFramework\Rest\Permission:

new PublicAccess()                      // everybody
new Capability('delete_posts')          // current_user_can('delete_posts')
new Callback(self::canEdit(...))        // your own check

A callback decides with your own logic. It is a first-class callable of a public static method that returns bool. It must be static because PHP allows first-class callables in attribute arguments only for static methods.

#[RestRoute('/{id}', [HttpMethod::Put, HttpMethod::Patch], new Callback(self::canEdit(...)))]
public function update(int $id, string $title): WP_REST_Response { /* … */ }

public static function canEdit(int $id, ItemRepository $items): bool
{
    return current_user_can('edit_post', $items->getPostId($id));
}

The callback's parameters follow the same rules as those of the route: services are injected, and request arguments must exist in the route with the same name and type. Before calling it, the framework validates and sanitizes these arguments against the route's own schema and denies access if one is invalid. That matters because WordPress also calls permission callbacks to build the Allow header, with a request validated for a different route handler.

Path placeholders

{name} in the path matches the parameter with the same name. That parameter must be required and of type int (matches \d+), string ([^/]+) or a backed enum (its values). Its value always comes from the URL, never from a query argument with the same name.

Route paths may only contain letters, digits, ., _, ~, -, / and placeholders.

Parameters

The framework looks at each parameter of the method and decides where its value comes from:

A service candidate is injected.

WP_REST_Request receives the request itself.

Everything else is a request argument with the parameter's name: int, float, string, bool, a backed enum, or an array with #[ListOf(Enum::class)] or #[ListOf(ValueClass::class)] (see Values). Each may be nullable and have a default value.

A single value class without #[ListOf] is not supported as a request argument, because a parameter with a class type is treated as a service.

From the request arguments the framework builds the route's argument schema (type, enum, items, required, default). WordPress then does the work it always does with a schema: it validates and sanitizes the arguments, answers with 400 if one is invalid, and shows the schema on an OPTIONS request. Missing optional arguments get the parameter's default. Enums, value objects and lists are converted by the value factory, so your method receives typed values.

#[Param] (Saij\WpAppFramework\Rest\Param) adds further constraints to the schema:

public function update(
    int $id,
    #[Param(maxLength: 200)] string $title,
    #[Param(format: Format::Email)] ?string $contact = null,
): WP_REST_Response

Its arguments are description, minimum, maximum, minLength, maxLength, pattern and format (a case of Saij\WpAppFramework\Rest\Format). The build checks that each one applies to the parameter's type.

Responses and errors

What the method returns decides the response:

A void method responds with 204 No Content.

Any other value goes through rest_ensure_response() and responds with 200.

For another status code or extra headers, return a WP_REST_Response, e.g. new WP_REST_Response($data, 201).

#[RestRoute('/{id}', HttpMethod::Delete, new Capability('delete_posts'))]
public function delete(int $id): void
{
    // … responds with 204 No Content
}

For an error response, throw RestException(code, message, status, data) with a status between 400 and 599. The response adds the status to the data, so data must not have a key status of its own; that is an InvalidArgumentException. Any other exception is an unexpected error. It is logged with error_log() and answered with status 500 and the code wp_app_framework_internal_error. Class, message, file, line and stack trace of the exception are included in the response only if WP_DEBUG is enabled, so a live site never shows its internals.

Like hooks, the controller and its services are created only when the route is called.

Caching

A GET route can keep its response with #[Cache], plain data or a WP_REST_Response with a status below 400: the arguments of the method are part of the key, the permission check still runs on every request, and errors are never stored. See Cache.

title: Services

toc.text: Only what is used is built

description: Most classes in a theme or plugin need other classes: a hook needs a formatter, a block needs the template renderer, a REST route needs a repository. You don't create these objects yourself, and you don't register them anywhere. You ask for them in the constructor, and the framework's container passes them in. TitleFilter asks for a Formatter, so the container creates one and passes it in. Formatter needs no registration: it is a class in the theme's src/, which makes it a service.

title: Settings
content:
Settings are values for the whole site that a theme or plugin makes configurable in the backend: a tagline, the logo, the page with the privacy policy, the default density of lists. You describe them as typed classes, as you do with block attributes. The framework takes care of the rest: it stores each group of settings in a WordPress option, it adds a settings page with a form for all groups, it passes the values to your services and templates as typed objects. Settings that several blocks share but that are stored per block, such as a color scheme for each block, are block supports, not settings. Declaring a group Settings come in groups. A group is a readonly class with #[SettingsGroup], and each setting is a public promoted constructor parameter with a default: use Saij\WpAppFramework\Value\Image; use Saij\WpAppFramework\Value\Label; use Saij\WpAppFramework\Setting\SettingsGroup; use Saij\WpAppFramework\Value\ListOf; use Saij\WpAppFramework\Value\Url; #[SettingsGroup('general', title: 'General', description: 'Shown on every page.')] final readonly class GeneralSettings { /** * @param list $links */ public function __construct( #[Label('Tagline')] public string $tagline = '', public Density $density = Density::Normal, #[Url] public string $contactUrl = '', #[ListOf(SocialLink::class)] public array $links = [], #[Image] public ?int $logo = null, ) {} } The settings page shows this group as a form: a text field for the tagline, a select for the density, a URL field, a list editor for the social links, and an image picker for the logo. #[SettingsGroup(name, title, description: '', position: 10)] takes these arguments: name consists of lowercase letters, digits and _ and starts with a letter. It is unique within the theme or plugin, and it names the option and the key in templates. title is the title of the group on the settings page. description is an optional text above its form. position orders the groups: lower values first, then by name. Every setting needs a default, because a setting is missing until the group has been saved for the first time. Types of settings Settings follow the rules of values: int, float, string, bool, backed enums, value classes and #[ListOf] lists, each optionally nullable. Enum cases are labeled with Labeled. #[Url] and #[Label] work as for block attributes, and #[Hidden] keeps a setting off the settings page. Some markers from blocks have a meaning in settings too: #[Image] on a ?int stores the ID of an attachment, chosen from the media library. It also works in value classes and list items. Print the image with wp_attachment_image(). A value class used both by a block and by a settings group edits its image in the block canvas there and in the form here. #[PlainText] is a text field; with multiline: true a text area. Print multiline text with |nl2br. Link is a link to a post or a free URL, with "Open in new tab": a search of published posts and a URL field. Print it with link_attributes(). #[RichText(allowedFormats: null)] is edited with WordPress' classic editor, because the rich text of the block editor works only inside a block. allowedFormats may contain core/bold, core/italic, core/link, core/strikethrough, core/subscript and core/superscript; other formats are build errors. The editor keeps only these elements and line breaks, without paragraphs. Print rich text with |raw. When a user without unfiltered_html saves (for example on multisite), it is filtered with wp_kses_post(). References (#[PostReference], #[TermReference], #[UserReference]) are chosen with a search, one or as a list. Other markers do not fit: inspector and excerpt have no effect in settings. postContent is a build error. #[Content] marks the content of blocks and means nothing in settings. It is a build error, also in value classes that a group uses. A group class is not a service. It is created from the stored values, never autowired, and #[Hook] or other entry points on it are build errors. Storage Each group is stored in its own option, named {namespace}_{name}, where {namespace} is the namespace of the theme or plugin (extra.wp-app-framework.namespace) with _ instead of -. A theme with the namespace my-theme stores the group general in my_theme_general. The option holds an object with every setting of the group; settings missing from a saved object get their default. The framework registers the option with register_setting() on init, with its schema and show_in_rest. That makes it readable and writable through /wp/v2/settings under the same name. WordPress validates and sanitizes saved values against the schema there, and requires the capability manage_options for reading and saving. The option belongs to the theme's namespace, not to its directory name or the active stylesheet. A child theme without code therefore uses the settings of its parent theme, and switching to a child theme keeps them. A child theme with code and each plugin have their own groups and options. Deleting a plugin deletes the options of its groups (see Activation, deactivation and uninstallation); the options of a theme stay when the site switches to another theme. Using settings A service receives a group through its constructor: final class Footer { public function __construct(private readonly GeneralSettings $settings) {} #[Hook('wp_footer')] public function print(): void { printf('

%s

', esc_html($this->settings->tagline)); } } The group object is created from the stored values when it is first needed, and kept until the option changes. Groups can be injected into the constructors of services only, not as parameters of hooks, REST routes or template functions. Templates read the groups of their own theme or plugin through the global settings:

{{ settings.general.tagline }}

{{ wp_attachment_image(settings.general.logo, 'medium') }} settings exists only if the theme or plugin declares settings groups. An unknown group name is an error. Invalid stored values A stored value can stop matching its setting, for example when a case is removed from its enum. The framework replaces such a value with the setting's default and logs it (wp-app-framework: settings: … in the PHP error log). The other settings of the group keep their stored values, so one outdated value never resets the whole group. Settings page A theme or plugin with settings groups gets one settings page. Its title is the name of the theme or plugin: the Theme Name: header of style.css, or the Plugin Name: header of the plugin's main file. A missing name is a build error. Themes and child themes find the page under "Appearance", plugins under "Settings". Only users with manage_options can open it. Each group is a form built from the same controls as the block inspector: text, number, toggle, select, rich text, image from the media library, reference search, nested values and the list editor. Several groups appear as tabs; a tab with unsaved changes is marked with "•". One "Save" button saves all groups in a single request through /wp/v2/settings. If a value is invalid, WordPress rejects the whole request, the page names the group and the setting, and nothing is saved. The page script is built by the theme's or plugin's build, like the editor runtime (see Editor), to build/vendor/wp-app-framework/settings.js. Without it, the settings page fails with an exception naming the missing file.

title: Styles
description: Block markup is styled with Tailwind CSS 4. The work is split between the framework and the theme. The framework compiles the stylesheet and loads it on the front end and in the editor. The design – which Tailwind tokens exist and which WordPress values they point to – belongs to the theme. The framework ships no stylesheet for the front end of its own, because design tokens differ from theme to theme.

title: Block supports
content:
Some settings belong to many blocks at once. A color scheme is the typical example: a card, a section and a teaser should all offer the same choice, look the same in the inspector and produce the same class names. Copying an enum into every attribute class and a class into every template would work, but every new block would have to repeat it, and nothing would keep the copies in line.

A block support declares such a setting once. Every block that uses it gets an attribute, a control in the inspector and class names on its root element; the framework derives all of that in the build. WordPress uses the same idea for its own supports such as alignment, which you switch on with #[Supports].

Block supports apply only to the blocks of the same theme or plugin, not to core blocks or blocks of other instances. Values for the whole site rather than for a single block are settings.

Declaring a support

A support is a service class with #[BlockSupport] and a public method className(). The method receives the value of the attribute and returns the class names for it:

use Saij\WpAppFramework\Block\Support\BlockSupport;

#[BlockSupport('surface', label: 'Surface')]
final class Surface
{
    public function className(SurfaceTone $value = SurfaceTone::Light): ?string
    {
        return 'surface-' . $value->value;
    }
}

The signature of className() describes the whole support. Its parameter type sets the attribute's schema and the control in the inspector, and its default is the attribute's default. Here SurfaceTone is a backed enum, so the inspector shows a select, and blocks start with SurfaceTone::Light.

#[BlockSupport(attribute, label, group: SupportGroup::Styles)] takes three arguments:

attribute is the name of the block attribute, in camelCase (colorScheme). The names WordPress reserves (lock, metadata, className, anchor, align, style) and a name that another support of the same theme or plugin uses are build errors.

label labels the control.

group places the control in the "Styles" tab (SupportGroup::Styles) or in the block's "Settings" panel (SupportGroup::Settings).

className() has exactly one parameter, with a default. Its type is one of these, each optionally nullable:

Type	Control
backed enum	select; label the cases with Labeled
bool	toggle
int, float	number
string	text

Value classes and lists are not supported, and the parameter takes no attributes such as #[Label]. The method returns string or ?string: the class names for the value, several separated by spaces, or null or '' for none.

The class is a service. It can depend on other services through its constructor – for example to read the available color schemes from the settings – and it is created when a block with the support renders for the first time. A support that no block uses is not built.

Using a support

A block adds a support with #[UseSupport]. It is repeatable, one per support:

#[Block('card', title: 'Card', category: BlockCategory::Design)]
#[UseSupport(Surface::class, default: SurfaceTone::Dark)]
final class Card
{
    public function render(CardAttributes $attrs): string { /* … */ }
}

The block now has the attribute surface. Its default comes from the parameter of className(); default overrides it for this block and must have the type of the value – a case of the enum, a bool, and so on.

The template doesn't need to know about the support. It prints the root element with block_wrapper_attributes(), as every block template does, and that adds the class names of all supports to the classes of WordPress' supports:

<article {{ block_wrapper_attributes({class: 'card'}) }}>…</article>

A block with supports that renders without calling block_wrapper_attributes() fails. That way a support never stays without effect unnoticed.

Like every attribute, the value is stored in the block comment, e.g. <!-- wp:sections/card {"surface":"light"} /-->. The attribute object passed to render() does not contain it; the support handles it.

The following are build errors: an attribute of a support with the name of a parameter of the block's attribute class, the same support used twice, and a class without #[BlockSupport] in #[UseSupport].

At render time

Before the block renders, the framework sanitizes the value against its schema, converts it to its PHP type (an enum case, for example) and calls className().

Each returned class name must consist of letters, digits, - and _, so it must equal its sanitize_html_class(). Anything else is an error, because a class name built from user data could otherwise break the markup. Errors are handled like the render errors of blocks: rethrown with WP_DEBUG, otherwise logged, and the block renders nothing.

Blocks rendered for an excerpt evaluate no supports.

In the editor

The control appears in the support's group, only in the default editing mode. In contentOnly mode – in patterns and template parts – it is hidden, as WordPress hides its own design settings there. Changing the value renders the block again, so the class names in the canvas come from the server, just like on the front end.

A script next to the support class can replace the generated control in every block that uses the support. For src/Support/Surface.php that is src/Support/Surface.editor.js; it is loaded with the runtime if a block uses the support:

registerSupportControl( 'surface', ( { value, onChange } ) => <SurfacePicker value={ value } onChange={ onChange } /> );

The component receives { value, onChange, attributes, setAttributes, clientId, isPreview }. A control that a block registers with registerControl() for the same attribute wins over the support's control.

On the front end

When a support needs JavaScript on the page – an element that fades in while it scrolls into view, for example – put a view script next to its class: src/Support/Reveal.view.js. It runs in every block that uses the support and receives the support's value. See Front-end scripts.

Styling

className() builds class names at run time, so Tailwind does not find them in the templates. Style them with CSS of the theme, or list them with @source inline(…) in assets/styles.css (see Styles).
description: Some settings belong to many blocks at once. A color scheme is the typical example: a card, a section and a teaser should all offer the same choice, look the same in the inspector and produce the same class names. Copying an enum into every attribute class and a class into every template would work, but every new block would have to repeat it, and nothing would keep the copies in line. A block support declares such a setting once. Every block that uses it gets an attribute, a control in the inspector and class names on its root element; the framework derives all of that in the build. WordPress uses the same idea for its own supports such as alignment, which you switch on with #[Supports]. Block supports apply only to the blocks of the same theme or plugin, not to core blocks or blocks of other instances. Values for the whole site rather than for a single block are settings.

title: Tables
content:
Some data does not fit into posts: a log of imports, counters, assignments between objects, the state of a background job. Each of them has many rows with the same few columns, is rarely edited by hand and does not need revisions, URLs or the block editor. Stored as posts with meta fields, every row would cost a post and one meta row per field, and a query would join the meta table once per condition. A table of its own is faster and simpler.

In plain WordPress you would write the CREATE TABLE yourself, keep it up to date with dbDelta() and read rows as arrays of strings with $wpdb. The framework lets you declare a table as a class instead. It creates the table, changes it when the class changes, and loads and saves rows as objects – the same way post classes work for posts.

$entry = new LogEntry(level: Level::Error, message: 'Import failed');
$entry->save();

$errors = LogEntry::query()
    ->where(LogEntryFields::level()->equals(Level::Error))
    ->orderBy(LogEntryFields::created(), Direction::Desc)
    ->limit(20)
    ->get();

Use posts for content that people edit, link to or translate; use a table for data your code writes and reads.

The row class

A row class extends AbstractRow and carries #[Table] with the name of the table. Its promoted constructor parameters are the columns:

use Saij\WpAppFramework\Table\{AbstractRow, Table, PrimaryKey, Indexed, Length, Text};

#[Table('log')]
final class LogEntry extends AbstractRow
{
    public function __construct(
        #[PrimaryKey]
        private ?int $id = null,
        #[Indexed(group: 'level_created', position: 1)]
        private Level $level = Level::Info,
        #[Length(500)]
        private string $message = '',
        #[Text]
        private string $context = '',
        #[Indexed]
        private ?int $postId = null,
        #[Indexed(group: 'level_created', position: 2)]
        private DateTimeImmutable $created = new DateTimeImmutable(),
    ) {}

    public function getId(): ?int
    {
        return $this->id;
    }

    public function setLevel(Level $level): void
    {
        $this->level = $level;
    }

    // further getters and setters …
}

The table is called {prefix}{namespace}_{name}: with the table prefix wp_ and the namespace dev-test of your composer.json, wp_dev_test_log. A theme and a plugin therefore never share a table, even if both name it log.

Each column is named after its parameter in snake case: $postId becomes the column post_id. The parameters are private or protected; you decide with getters and setters what the rest of your code may read and change.

Types

The type of a parameter decides the type of its column. A nullable type (?int) allows NULL; otherwise the column is NOT NULL.

PHP	Column
int	bigint(20)
float	double
bool	tinyint(1)
string	varchar(191); with #[Length(n)] varchar(n); with #[Text] longtext
backed enum	the value of the case: varchar(191) for string enums, bigint(20) for int enums
DateTimeImmutable	datetime, in UTC
#[PrimaryKey] ?int	bigint(20) unsigned with auto increment

A constant default of the parameter – a number, a string, null or an enum case – is the default of the column, too. Long text and times have no default in the table; new DateTimeImmutable() is evaluated by PHP when you create the object.

Floats are written with every digit, so a float you save is the float you load. Times are stored in UTC to the second; a time of another time zone is converted when it is saved.

Indexes

#[Indexed] gives the column an index of its own, named after the column. Add unique: true for a unique index. An index over several columns is a group: give each column the group name and its position.

#[Indexed(group: 'level_created', position: 1)]
private Level $level = Level::Info,
// …
#[Indexed(group: 'level_created', position: 2)]
private DateTimeImmutable $created = new DateTimeImmutable(),

The primary key has its index already. Long text and strings longer than 191 characters cannot be indexed: MariaDB and MySQL limit an index to 3072 bytes, and a character takes up to four.

Loading, saving and deleting

A new row is an object you create with new. save() inserts it and sets its primary key:

$entry = new LogEntry(level: Level::Error, message: 'Import failed', postId: $post->getId());
$entry->save();
$id = $entry->getId();

get() loads a row by its primary key and throws an exception if there is none; find() returns null instead. After a change, save() writes only the columns that changed. Without a change, it writes nothing.

$entry = LogEntry::get($id);
$entry->setLevel(Level::Info);
$entry->save();

$entry->delete();   // its primary key is null afterwards

You can also create a row object with a primary key of your own, for example to restore a row you exported. save() writes it like a loaded row: it updates the row with that key, and if there is none, it inserts the row with that key and all columns.

new LogEntry(id: 42, level: Level::Error, message: 'Restored')->save();

The same happens when the row of a loaded object was deleted in the meantime and you change and save the object: the row comes back with its old primary key. Finding out whether the row exists costs a query of its own, but only when the update changed nothing. MariaDB and MySQL count only the rows an UPDATE really changed, so an update of a row that already has these values looks the same as an update of a missing row.

Every get(), find() and query returns new objects. When two of them change the same row, each save() writes its changed columns; for a column changed by both, the last one wins. save() and delete() check no capabilities.

If the database refuses a row – a string longer than its column, for example – save() throws a RuntimeException with the error of the database. A stored value that no longer fits the class, such as the value of a removed enum case, makes loading the row throw an exception; the framework does not quietly use the default instead.

Queries

LogEntry::query() starts a query of rows. It works like a query of posts: it never changes, so keep the result of each method, and it takes conditions from field objects and the groups Any and All.

$rows = LogEntry::query()
    ->where(LogEntryFields::created()->greaterThan(new DateTimeImmutable('-1 day')))
    ->where(Any::of(
        LogEntryFields::level()->equals(Level::Error),
        All::of(LogEntryFields::attempts()->greaterThan(3), LogEntryFields::postId()->isNotNull()),
    ))
    ->orderBy(LogEntryFields::created(), Direction::Desc)
    ->limit(20)
    ->get();

The framework writes the SQL of the query itself, with every value passed through $wpdb->prepare(). Groups can contain groups to any depth. Without orderBy(), rows come in the order of their primary key.

count() counts all matching rows. delete() deletes them and returns how many – with limit() only the first ones in the order of the query:

$removed = LogEntry::query()->where(LogEntryFields::created()->lessThan($cutoff))->delete();

Field classes

As with meta fields, the field objects come from a class of their own, marked #[TableFields]. Let the framework write it:

vendor/bin/wp-app-framework table-fields 'Sections\Table\LogEntry'

The command writes LogEntryFields.php next to the row class, with one method per column:

#[TableFields(LogEntry::class)]
final class LogEntryFields
{
    /**
     * @return EnumField<Level>
     */
    public static function level(): EnumField
    {
        return new EnumField(LogEntry::class, 'level', Level::class);
    }

    public static function postId(): NullableIntField
    {
        return new NullableIntField(LogEntry::class, 'postId');
    }

    // …
}

The file is ordinary source code, like the one of meta-fields: commit it, shorten it, or write it by hand. The build checks every method that returns a field. A column that allows NULL needs the Nullable… variant of its field class, which adds isNull() and isNotNull(); any other column needs the plain class.

Null

A nullable column without a value holds NULL. Conditions on it behave like comparisons in PHP: equals(5) does not find a row without value, and notEquals(5) and notIn(…) do find it, because null !== 5. Plain SQL would leave such rows out of both; the framework adds OR … IS NULL for you. Use isNull() and isNotNull() to ask for the missing value itself.

When you sort by a nullable column, rows without value come first in ascending order and last in descending order.

Strings are compared without regard to case, like the collation of WordPress' tables.

SQL of your own

For anything a query cannot express – joins, sums, groups – write SQL yourself. LogEntry::tableName() returns the full name of the table on the current site:

global $wpdb;
$counts = $wpdb->get_results($wpdb->prepare(
    'SELECT level, COUNT(*) AS count FROM %i GROUP BY level',
    LogEntry::tableName(),
));

Rows you change this way bypass the row objects; objects loaded before keep their values.

Keeping tables up to date

The framework creates and changes the tables itself; you never write CREATE TABLE or ALTER TABLE. The build stores the structure of all tables of your theme or plugin in its manifest, together with a hash of it. On init, the framework compares that hash with the one stored after the last change of the tables. This comparison reads an option WordPress loads anyway, so a request whose tables are current costs no database query.

When the hashes differ, the framework syncs the tables of the current site:

It creates every table that does not exist.

It compares each table with its class and changes it in one ALTER TABLE: it adds missing columns and indexes, changes columns whose type, NULL or default differ, renames columns, and drops columns and indexes the class does not declare.

It reads the table again; a remaining difference is an error.

It drops the tables of row classes you removed.

Every change goes to the error log with the prefix wp-app-framework: tables:.

The sync makes the tables match your classes, also when that loses data, and also in development mode – switching to a branch with fewer columns drops them:

A removed parameter drops its column; a removed row class drops its table.

A renamed parameter is a new column; the old one and its data are dropped. Rename with #[RenamedFrom], a table with renamedFrom of #[Table].

A shorter #[Length] cuts longer values. A column that becomes NOT NULL gets 0, an empty string or the zero date where it held NULL; the log says how many values changed.

Keep #[RenamedFrom] as long as an installation may still have the old column.

Renaming

#[RenamedFrom('text')] names an earlier name of the parameter. If the table has a column of that name and none of the new name, the sync renames it, and the data stays. For a parameter renamed several times, add one attribute per earlier name, newest first.

#[RenamedFrom('text')]
private string $message = '',

If both columns exist – after a manual change, for example – the sync leaves the old one alone and logs it, so you can merge them by hand.

A table is renamed the same way: #[Table('entries', renamedFrom: ['log'])] renames wp_dev_test_log if wp_dev_test_entries does not exist yet.

The sync drops only tables it created itself, and only in the current namespace. If you change the namespace of your theme or plugin, the tables of the old namespace stay and the log names them.

When the sync does not run

A sync changes tables that other requests use at the same time, so it takes a lock first. A request that finds the tables locked leaves them to the request that holds the lock.

During a deployment, an older version of your code may still run next to the new one. That code must not undo the changes of the new one. The framework therefore stores the version of your theme or plugin (the Version: header) with the tables and does not sync them for code with a lower version. If you roll back to an older version on purpose, the tables stay as the newer version left them.

If a sync fails, the framework writes the error to the log and tries again after five minutes. With WP_DEBUG, a failure on init is thrown.

Code that uses a table while its sync cannot run – locked, failed or blocked by the version – gets a RuntimeException that names the reason. Code that runs before init, or after switch_to_blog() on another site, syncs the tables before it uses them. While WordPress installs, nothing is synced.

Multisite

Each site has its own tables, with the table prefix of the site. The sync runs for a site on the first request to it, or when code switches to it with switch_to_blog() and uses a table. There are no tables shared by the network. When a site is deleted, its tables of your plugin are dropped with it.

Removing tables

The tables of a theme stay when the site switches to another theme, so they are there again when it switches back. When a plugin is deleted, the framework drops its tables on every site – also tables an earlier namespace of the plugin left – and deletes the state of their sync. See Activation, deactivation and uninstallation.

Rules

#[Table(name, renamedFrom: [])] on a class that extends AbstractRow:

name and each earlier name: lowercase letters, digits and _, starting with a letter; unique among the tables of the theme or plugin. {namespace}_{name} has at most 50 characters.

The class is concrete and has a public constructor of its own. Every constructor parameter is a promoted property, private or protected; the class declares no other properties.

Exactly one parameter has #[PrimaryKey]: ?int with the default null, not readonly.

Types: int, float, bool, string, backed enums and DateTimeImmutable, each also nullable. Not: arrays, other objects, DateTime, DateTimeInterface, union types, mixed.

Parameters take #[PrimaryKey], #[Indexed], #[RenamedFrom], #[Length] and #[Text] only. Column names are unique and have at most 64 characters.

#[Length(n)]: string columns, 1 to 16383; a default must fit. #[Text]: string columns, not together with #[Length]. Values of string enums have at most 191 characters.

#[Indexed(group, position, unique)]: not on the primary key, long text or strings longer than 191 characters. A group needs a position and vice versa; positions are 1 to n without gaps; unique is the same for every column of a group. Group names follow the rules of table names (not primary), have at most 64 characters and differ from the columns with an index of their own. Two indexes with the same columns are an error, and so is an index of more than 3072 bytes.

A row has at most 65535 bytes without long text, as MariaDB and MySQL count them.

#[RenamedFrom(column)]: an earlier parameter name; not the current one, not the name of another column, not twice in the class.

A class that extends AbstractRow without #[Table] is an error. Row classes are no services and cannot be injected or passed to hooks or routes.

AbstractRow:

Method	Effect
static get(int $id)	The row; InvalidArgumentException if there is none.
static find(int $id)	The row or null.
static query()	A RowQuery of the class.
static tableName()	The full table name on the current site.
save()	Inserts the row and sets the primary key, or writes the changed columns; without changes, nothing. With a primary key whose row does not exist, inserts the row with that key and all columns. RuntimeException if the database refuses it, e.g. a duplicate key when another request inserted the row first.
delete()	Deletes the row; the primary key becomes null. LogicException for a row that was never saved.

All of them work once the theme or plugin has booted; before, they throw a LogicException.

RowQuery (every method that returns a query is #[\NoDiscard]):

Method	Effect
where(Condition ...$conditions)	All conditions must be met; adds to earlier calls. Conditions on columns of the class only.
orderBy(Field $field, Direction = Asc)	Sorts; further calls sort what is still equal. Without it: by primary key.
limit(int), offset(int)	At most this many rows (at least 1), skipping some (with limit()).
get()	The rows, as objects of the row class.
first()	The first row or null.
count()	The number of all matching rows, regardless of limit() and offset().
delete()	Deletes the matching rows (with limit() the first ones) and returns their number; not with offset().

As in post queries, a value outside the allowed range, such as limit(0), throws an InvalidArgumentException when you call the method. A combination that does not fit, offset() without limit() in get() or offset() in delete(), throws a LogicException when the query runs.

Columns and their field classes:

Column	Field class	Conditions
string	StringField	equals, notEquals, in, notIn, greaterThan, greaterOrEqual, lessThan, lessOrEqual, between, contains
int, primary key	IntField	as StringField, without contains
float	FloatField	as IntField
bool	BoolField	equals
backed enum	EnumField<E>	equals, notEquals, in, notIn
DateTimeImmutable	DateTimeField	as IntField, with DateTimeInterface
nullable (?string, …)	NullableStringField, NullableIntField, NullableFloatField, NullableBoolField, NullableEnumField<E>, NullableDateTimeField	as above, and isNull, isNotNull

#[TableFields(rowClass)] on a class of your own: one class per row class; every public static method that returns a field has no parameters and returns a field of rowClass with an existing column and its field class (with the enum of the column). The class is no service. In development mode the build runs again when signatures change, not when only a method body changes; a query checks its fields again when it runs.

wp-app-framework table-fields <row class> [--force] writes {RowClass}Fields.php next to the row class. An existing file is replaced only with --force.
