title: Twig templates
content: Markup in the framework lives in Twig templates, not in PHP strings. Twig escapes every value by default, so you don't have to remember esc_html() for each one; only |raw and functions marked HTML print a value unescaped. It also keeps markup readable, and it lets child themes and themes override the markup of a block without touching its code. Twig renders the markup of blocks and fragments your code produces, such as the body of a mail or an HTML response. Page layouts are not Twig; they are block templates and template parts, as in any block theme. Where templates live Templates sit in the src/ directory of the theme or plugin, next to the code that uses them (src/Hook/Mail.twig, src/Block/Hero/Hero.twig), or in shared directories (src/Component/Button.twig). There is no separate views/ directory. A template name is always the full path relative to src/, including the extension: 'Component/Button.twig'. That holds in PHP and in templates alike. There are no relative names, so a name means the same thing wherever it appears. Rendering a template A service renders a template through the TemplateRenderer, which it asks for in its constructor. render(name, context) returns the HTML as a string: use Saij\WpAppFramework\Hook\Hook; use Saij\WpAppFramework\Twig\TemplateRenderer; final class Mail { public function __construct(private readonly TemplateRenderer $renderer) { } #[Hook('sections_mail_body')] public function body(string $body, string $name): string { return $this->renderer->render('Hook/Mail.twig', ['body' => $body, 'name' => $name]); } } The Twig environment is created when the first template renders, so a request without templates pays nothing for it. Blocks render their templates the same way (see Blocks). Lookup A template name without a namespace is searched in several layers. The first layer that has the file wins: overrides/{theme-slug}/ of the active child theme, if it has that directory, the theme's src/, the framework's src/. A higher layer overrides a template by providing a file with the same path. For example, a child theme of my-theme changes the markup of the theme's hero block, src/Block/Hero/Hero.twig, with its own overrides/my-theme/Block/Hero/Hero.twig. The theme's PHP code stays as it is. Sometimes you need exactly one layer, for example when an override extends the original template it replaces. @theme/… and @framework/… address exactly that layer and cannot be overridden: {% include 'Component/Button.twig' %} {# child overrides → theme → framework #} {% include '@framework/Component/Button.twig' %} {# exactly this layer #} wp-app-framework build lists the project's templates that override framework templates. Child themes and plugins The src/ of a child theme belongs to its own framework instance, if it boots one. Its templates are searched in its own src/, then in the framework's, and they never override templates of the theme. To override the theme, a child theme uses overrides/{theme-slug}/. A plugin's templates are searched in this order: overrides/{plugin-slug}/ of the child theme, overrides/{plugin-slug}/ of the theme, the plugin's src/, the framework's src/. A theme overrides src/Block/Note/Note.twig of the plugin my-plugin with overrides/my-plugin/Block/Note/Note.twig. Because overrides live in their own directory, the theme's templates in src/ never collide with the plugin's. @plugin/… addresses the plugin's own templates exactly. The plugin's Twig environment renders the override. The override therefore sees the plugin's template functions and filters and the context the plugin passes, not those of the theme. Compiled templates are named after the slug of their instance, so a theme and a plugin never share compiled code of templates with the same path. Environment Twig runs with settings that catch mistakes early: Autoescaping (html) is always on. strict_variables is always on, so an undefined variable is an error instead of an empty string. In development mode, debug, auto reload and dump() are enabled; in release mode they are off. A theme or plugin with settings groups has the global settings (see Settings). The framework provides the template functions of blocks (block_wrapper_attributes(), see Blocks), of the editor (field(), inner_blocks(), is_editor(), see Editor), has_plugin() (see Plugins), post() for post objects (see Posts), link_attributes() for links, asset_url(), asset_image() and asset_svg() for the files in assets/ (see Static assets) and the WordPress functions below. Twig exceptions reach the code that rendered the template, so the error handling of hooks and REST routes applies to them. Cache Compiled templates are cached in wp-content/cache/{slug}/twig/. Release mode compiles without auto reload: Twig never checks whether a template changed. Each release therefore uses its own directory, wp-content/cache/{slug}/twig/{templateVersion}/. The template version is a hash over the names and contents of all templates of the project and the framework; build --output writes it into the release manifest. Overrides add one more level. If the active theme or child theme overrides templates of another instance – a plugin, or the theme overridden by its child theme – that instance's cache directory gets a further level named after the versions of theme and child theme. A changed override therefore needs a new version of the theme or child theme. Directories of older releases are removed by a daily WP-Cron event, the same event that cleans up the file cache. It keeps the directory of the current template version and, below it, the directory of the current theme and child theme versions. On multisite, all sites share the cache directory but may run other themes, so the event keeps the override directories of the current release; they go with the next release. Template functions and filters Your own Twig functions and filters are methods of services with #[TemplateFunction] or #[TemplateFilter]: use Saij\WpAppFramework\Twig\TemplateFilter; use Saij\WpAppFramework\Twig\TemplateFunction; final class Formatting { #[TemplateFunction('price')] public function price(int $cents): string { return number_format($cents / 100, 2, ',', '.') . ' €'; } #[TemplateFilter('highlight', html: true)] public function highlight(string $value): string { return '' . $value . ''; } } {{ price(total) }} {{ name|highlight }} The service is created when a template calls one of its functions for the first time. Like other services, it gets its dependencies through its constructor. Escaping By default Twig escapes the result of a function or filter. A method that returns HTML sets html: true; its result is printed as it is, and it must return string. An HTML filter receives the filtered value already HTML-escaped, unless the value is safe already (for example after |raw). Twig's nl2br works the same way. In the example, highlight can wrap $value in without escaping it first. Other arguments are passed unescaped: an HTML function or filter must escape every argument it puts into its result. Rules #[TemplateFunction(name, html: false, public: false)] and #[TemplateFilter(name, html: false, public: false)] go on public, non-static methods of services. Names are valid identifiers and unique per kind. They must not reuse a function or filter Twig provides, because Twig would silently replace it. Parameters must not be services (inject them through the constructor), variadic or by reference. A filter receives the filtered value as its first parameter. Callables offered to other consumers (public: true) are described in Plugins. WordPress functions Templates often need data from WordPress: an image for an attachment ID, the title and URL of a linked post, the site name. The framework provides these as template functions. Each is a thin wrapper around a WordPress function, and the wp_ prefix tells you so at a glance. {{ wp_post_title(attrs.target) }} {{ wp_attachment_image(attrs.imageId, 'large', { class: 'rounded' }) }} {{ wp_post_date(attrs.target, 'j. F Y') }} The names follow one rule: wp_ + object + property, without get_ or the_. A WordPress function that already starts with wp_ keeps its name (wp_date, not wp_wp_date). The prefix is not reserved for the framework, but a name the framework already uses is a build error. The functions handle missing data for you: IDs may be null, for example an empty #[Image] or reference. null and objects that do not exist give '', so a template does not need to check first. Posts that are not publicly viewable count as missing, except when the block editor renders the block: a draft, or a post of a type that is not public. Attachments are not checked for visibility. post() checks only the status, so it also returns posts of your data types (see Posts). Text is escaped by Twig. Some values come from WordPress already escaped: term and user names, the site name and description, and the logout URL. The framework decodes them first, so they are not escaped twice. Functions marked HTML below print their result unescaped. Function WordPress Result wp_attachment_image(id, size = 'full', attributes = {}) wp_get_attachment_image() HTML wp_attachment_image_url(id, size = 'full') wp_get_attachment_image_url() URL wp_attachment_url(id) wp_get_attachment_url() URL wp_attachment_caption(id) wp_get_attachment_caption() HTML as stored (filtered with kses when saved without unfiltered_html) wp_attachment_alt(id) meta _wp_attachment_image_alt text wp_post_url(id) get_permalink() URL wp_post_title(id) post_title text wp_post_excerpt(id) get_the_excerpt() plain text: tags removed, entities decoded wp_post_date(id, format = '') get_the_date() text; '' uses the date format of the site wp_post_thumbnail(id, size = 'post-thumbnail', attributes = {}) get_the_post_thumbnail() HTML wp_term_url(id) get_term_link() URL wp_term_name(id) name of the term text wp_user_name(id) display_name of the user text wp_user_url(id) get_author_posts_url() URL of the author archive wp_avatar(id, size = 96) get_avatar() HTML; '' if avatars are turned off wp_home_url(path = '') home_url() URL wp_site_name() get_bloginfo('name') text wp_site_description() get_bloginfo('description') text wp_login_url(redirect = '') wp_login_url() URL wp_logout_url(redirect = '') wp_logout_url() URL with a nonce wp_is_user_logged_in() is_user_logged_in() true/false wp_date(format, timestamp = null) wp_date() text in the site's time zone and language; null for now wp_human_time_diff(from, to = 0) human_time_diff() text, e.g. "5 minutes"; 0 for now wp_number_format(number, decimals = 0) number_format_i18n() text wp_size_format(bytes, decimals = 0) size_format() text, e.g. "2 KB" The output of wp_logout_url() (a nonce), wp_is_user_logged_in() (the login state), wp_date() without a timestamp and wp_human_time_diff() without a second timestamp (the current time) depends on the request, not only on the attributes of a block. In cached blocks the framework checks them. Links link_attributes(link) prints the attributes of an element for a Link, like block_wrapper_attributes() prints those of the root element: {% if attrs.cta.url %} More {% endif %} The result is href="https://example.org/about/", escaped with esc_url(), plus target="_blank" rel="noopener" if the link opens in a new tab. For a link without URL – also a link to content that no longer exists or is not public – it prints nothing, so check link.url before you print the element. The function takes no further attributes; write classes and other attributes next to it.
description: Markup in the framework lives in Twig templates, not in PHP strings. Twig escapes every value by default, so you don't have to remember esc_html() for each one; only |raw and functions marked HTML print a value unescaped. It also keeps markup readable, and it lets child themes and themes override the markup of a block without touching its code. Twig renders the markup of blocks and fragments your code produces, such as the body of a mail or an HTML response. Page layouts are not Twig; they are block templates and template parts, as in any block theme.

title: Values
content: Blocks, REST routes and settings all deal with structured values: a headline, a choice among variants, a list of buttons, a link to another page. In WordPress these arrive as untyped arrays, either from the block comment, the request or an option. The framework lets you describe them once, as typed PHP classes, and uses that description in two places: In the build, it derives a JSON schema from the class. WordPress uses the schema to validate block attributes, REST arguments and settings. At run time, the value factory turns the stored array into an instance of your class, with enums as enum cases and nested objects as objects. It does this without reflection. Block attribute classes, settings groups, nested value classes and #[ListOf] REST arguments all work this way, so what you learn here applies to all of them. The data of a one-time cron task is a value class too, without references. Value classes A value class is a readonly class whose values are all public promoted constructor parameters: final readonly class Button { public function __construct( #[PlainText] public string $label, #[Url] public string $url = '', public ButtonStyle $style = ButtonStyle::Primary, ) {} } It declares no other properties. Elsewhere in the framework, class properties are never public; value classes are the exception, because they are plain data. Types A value can have one of these types, each optionally nullable: PHP type Schema int, float, string, bool integer, number, string, boolean backed enum the type of its values, with enum listing the case values value class object with properties array with #[ListOf(Enum::class)] or #[ListOf(ValueClass::class)] array with items A nullable type adds null to the schema type (type: [..., 'null']). PHP has no generic types, so a list says what it contains with #[ListOf]. Lists of scalars exist only for references. Enums and value classes must be in the scanned PSR-4 directories. A value class that contains itself, directly or indirectly, is a build error. The columns of tables use the same value factory with one more type: DateTimeImmutable, read from the database as a UTC time Y-m-d H:i:s. Anything else in such a column, including the zero date 0000-00-00 00:00:00, is an error. Blocks, REST routes and settings have no time type. Defaults and missing values The default value of a parameter becomes the schema's default: enums as their value, value objects as arrays. A missing value uses the constructor's default. Inside a nested value class, a parameter without a default is required in the schema. Unknown keys in nested objects are ignored, just as WordPress ignores unknown block attributes. Wrong values The value factory never coerces silently. A value that does not match its type throws an InvalidArgumentException that names the path to the value, for example buttons[1].url. Blocks, REST routes and settings each decide what happens next; see their pages. URLs #[Url] on a string adds format: uri to the schema, so the value is sanitized with sanitize_url(). Disallowed protocols such as javascript: become an empty string. Links A call to action, a link in a footer setting, a registration link of an event: a link points either to content of the site or to any address. #[Url] stores the address as text, so a link to a page breaks when someone changes the page's slug. A Link (namespace Saij\WpAppFramework\Value\) stores the ID of the page instead, and the framework looks up its current URL when it renders – the same idea as references, plus a URL entered freely and "Open in new tab". use Saij\WpAppFramework\Value\Label; use Saij\WpAppFramework\Value\Link; final readonly class TeaserAttributes { public function __construct( #[Label('Call to action')] public Link $cta = new Link(), ) {} } A link is never null. A new Link() has an empty URL, and an empty URL means "no link". Print it with link_attributes(), which writes href and, for a new tab, target and rel: {% if attrs.cta.url %} More {% endif %} Linked content and free URLs Editors choose the target in the block inspector with the link control of the block editor. It searches posts, terms and media files. A chosen result stays synced: the link stores its kind and ID, and the input field is locked until the editor chooses "Unsync and edit". An address typed into the field is a free URL: it is stored as it is, without ID. A link is stored as four values: {"url":"https://example.org/about/","opensInNewTab":true,"kind":"post","id":42} {"url":"https://example.com/","opensInNewTab":false,"kind":"url","id":0} kind is a LinkKind: Url for a free URL, Post, Term or Attachment for linked content. For linked content, the stored URL is only what the editor showed when the target was chosen; templates never see it. Resolution When the value is created, a linked post, term or media file gets its current URL: the permalink of a post, the archive of a term, the file of a media item. A link becomes empty – an empty url, while kind and id stay – if its target: no longer exists, is of a post type or taxonomy that is not viewable, is a post or media file that is not publicly viewable, such as a draft or the attachment of a draft. Renders for the block editor keep posts and media files that are not public, so editors still see what they chose. Free URLs stay as they are; like #[Url], they are sanitized with sanitize_url(). Resolving costs about as much as a reference: one lookup of the object, usually from the object cache, and one call for its URL. A cached block keeps the resolved URL until its cache entry is invalidated. If the URLs of linked pages matter, tag the block with the types it links to, for example PostTypeTag(Page::class), as you would for references. In templates and patterns of your theme, use free URLs only. IDs of pages, terms and media files differ from site to site, and the build does not check them. Outside the block editor The settings page and meta boxes on the classic edit screen do not load the block editor. There a link is edited with a form of its own: a search of published posts, which links the chosen post with its ID, a field for a free URL and the toggle "Open in new tab". A linked post shows its title and can be unlinked, which keeps its current URL as a free URL. Links to terms and media files are chosen in the block editor only. Rules Rule Type Link, never nullable; default new Link() Allowed in block attributes, value classes, lists (#[ListOf(Link::class)]), settings groups, meta classes Schema object with url (format: uri), opensInNewTab, kind (enum url, post, term, attachment) and id Blocks counts as content (role: content), editable in contentOnly mode Kind and ID kind: url with id: 0; any other kind with a positive ID The following are build errors: ?Link: a link is never null; an empty URL means no link; #[Content], #[Url], #[PlainText], #[RichText], #[Image] or a reference on a Link: a link is content with its own control. A stored link whose kind and ID do not match is a wrong value. The build checks links in templates and patterns against the schema, so a wrong kind or a string as opensInNewTab is an error there; it does not check whether an ID exists. References A block that links to another page, a setting that names the privacy policy page, a teaser that shows a category: these are references to WordPress objects. Storing the URL or the title would break as soon as someone renames the page. References store the ID instead, and the framework looks up the current data when it renders. #[PostReference(postTypes: null)], #[TermReference(taxonomies: null)] and #[UserReference] (namespace Saij\WpAppFramework\Value\) mark such IDs in block attributes, value classes and settings groups: #[PostReference(postTypes: ['page'])] public ?int $target = null, // one page, null without #[PostReference] public array $featured = [], // a list of post IDs, in order (list) #[TermReference(taxonomies: ['category'])] public ?int $topic = null, #[UserReference] public ?int $author = null, On ?int the parameter holds one reference, or null if nothing is chosen. On array it holds a list of IDs in the chosen order; there is no #[ListOf] for it. The schema is integer or ["integer", "null"], or an array of integers. postTypes and taxonomies limit the choice to these keys; null allows all viewable post types or taxonomies. The build does not check the keys against the registered types, because types are registered at run time. The search in the editor accepts only searchable post types and taxonomies. In blocks, a reference counts as content (role: content), like #[Image]. Post objects A parameter typed as a post class – a class with #[PostType], or the framework's Post and Page – is a reference too, without an attribute: it stores the ID and gives you the post object. public ?Event $event = null, // the event, null without #[ListOf(Venue::class)] public array $venues = [], // a list of venues (list) The single reference must be nullable. It resolves if the post has the type of the class and is published, also for post types that are not public, such as data types. The search in the editor uses the REST collection of the post type, so it finds posts of these types too. postTypes and taxonomies also take post and taxonomy classes instead of names: #[PostReference(postTypes: [Event::class, 'page'])], #[TermReference(taxonomies: [Genre::class, Category::class])]. WordPress' own types and taxonomies are the framework classes Post, Page, Category and Tag. Editing References are edited with a search, in the block inspector and on the settings page. Posts and terms are searched through /wp/v2/search, which finds published posts only. Users are searched through /wp/v2/users; users without the capability list_users see only authors of published posts. A list shows its entries as cards that can be moved up, moved down and removed. Resolution Content changes after a reference was stored. A page is deleted, or put back into draft. The framework checks this when it creates the value. A reference becomes null, or is left out of a list, if its target: no longer exists, is of another type, or not of a viewable type, is a post that is not publicly viewable. A deleted page therefore simply disappears from the output; nothing is logged. Renders for the block editor keep posts that are not public, such as drafts, so editors still see what they chose. Output The WordPress functions take the IDs: wp_post_title(id), wp_post_url(id), wp_term_name(id), wp_term_url(id), wp_user_name(id) and more. They return '' for null and missing objects. Posts that are not publicly viewable count as missing outside the editor. {% if attrs.target %} {{ wp_post_title(attrs.target) }} {% endif %} Rules The following are build errors: a reference on a type other than ?int or array, or together with #[ListOf]; a reference combined with #[PlainText], #[RichText], #[Image], #[Content] or #[Url]; several references on one parameter; empty or invalid postTypes or taxonomies; a reference on a REST argument. Declare the ID as int there. Where values are used Blocks, REST routes and Settings describe what each of them adds to these rules; Tables list the types of columns.

title: wp-app-framework
description: wp-app-framework is a PHP and JavaScript framework for building standalone full site editing themes, child themes and plugins for WordPress 7 on PHP 8.5. You write blocks, hooks, REST routes and settings as plain PHP classes with attributes. The framework turns them into everything WordPress expects: registered blocks with an attribute schema, an editor with inline editing, REST routes with validation, and a settings page. The framework is a library, not a theme or a plugin. Your theme, child theme or plugin includes it through Composer; the documentation calls these projects consumers. The framework registers no blocks itself; the blocks, hooks and routes you see in WordPress come from your code. Each consumer runs its own copy of the framework, called an instance. Its blocks, REST routes and settings are named after the consumer's namespace from composer.json; technical names – script handles, the JavaScript global, the cache directory, the init action – after its slug (its directory name). That is why a theme and several plugins can run side by side, even with different framework versions. Concepts explains this and the other ideas the guides build on.

title: Upgrading
content:
From 1.0 on, the consumer API only grows within a major version: nothing is renamed, removed or changed in behavior, and a theme built against 1.0 keeps working with 1.9. Before 1.0, a minor version may still break the API. This page lists every such change, why it was made, and what you need to change in your theme or plugin.

The documentation is published for each minor version. The version switcher in the navigation bar shows the documentation of other versions, so you can compare the old and the new state.

0.16

delete() moves posts of every type to the trash. AbstractPost::delete() used to call wp_delete_post(), which moves only posts and pages to the trash and deletes posts of other types permanently. Now delete() moves every post to the trash, so an editor can restore it (see Posts). Code that relied on permanent deletion of its own post types calls delete(true). A post already in the trash, and every post while the trash is disabled, is still deleted permanently.

RestException rejects a status in its data. The response always sets status to the status of the exception, so a key status in data was lost while getData() still returned it. It is now an InvalidArgumentException; pass the status as the third argument and remove the key from the data.

0.15

0.15 is the last review of the API before 1.0. It renames and tightens what would otherwise stay inconsistent for the whole 1.x series.

The field markers moved to Saij\WpAppFramework\Value. #[PlainText], #[RichText], #[Image], #[Label], #[Hidden], #[Content] and the interface Labeled are not only for blocks: settings groups, meta classes and value classes use them too. They now live next to #[ListOf], #[Url] and the references. Replace Saij\WpAppFramework\Block\ with Saij\WpAppFramework\Value\ in the use lines of these seven names; the old names no longer exist, so PHP or the build reports every place you missed.

#[CronTask] takes a name. The name of a task used to come from the short name of its class, so renaming the class silently dropped the planned tasks. Now you name it, like a recurring event: #[CronTask('send-reminder')] (see Cron events and tasks). To keep tasks that are already planned, use the name the framework derived before: the short class name in kebab case (SendReminder → send-reminder, HTMLExport → html-export). A #[CronTask] without a name is a build error.

The arguments of #[Variation] follow #[Block]. The order is now name, title, icon, description, keywords, …, as in #[Block]; icon and description swapped places. Only a variation that passes description or icon positionally is affected; name these arguments (icon: 'columns'), because the build cannot tell the two strings apart.

@saij/wp-app-framework is the editor API only. The import used to resolve to the whole global wpAppFramework[slug], so internal parts such as config were importable. It now resolves to wpAppFramework[slug].api, which holds registerControl(), registerSupportControl(), registerPanel(), registerToolbarButton(), loadScript() and getData() (see Editor). Code that imports only these needs no change. Code that called them on the global, window.wpAppFramework[slug].registerPanel(…), calls them on window.wpAppFramework[slug].api now. loadScript() of both imports takes two arguments, the URL and the attributes.

The webpack helper is @saij/wp-app-framework/webpack. The package declares its entry points now, with TypeScript declarations for both imports that your IDE picks up. Replace require( './vendor/saij/wp-app-framework/webpack.config.js' ) in your webpack.config.js with require( '@saij/wp-app-framework/webpack' ); the old path still works.

The release workflow input cli-tests is now cli. It goes with e2e (see Releases and CI). Rename it in the workflow of your project that calls consumer-release.yml.

Internal services cannot be injected. The render context of the editor (Editor\RenderContext) and the post store (Post\PostStore) are internal to the framework. A class of your theme or plugin that injects one of them is now a build error. Use the template functions is_editor(), field() and inner_blocks() in templates, and Event::get(), find() and query() for posts.

The framework is on Packagist. Composer finds saij/wp-app-framework without a repositories entry now. Remove the vcs entry for the framework from your composer.json and run composer update saij/wp-app-framework (see Releases and CI); a project that keeps the entry still works.

The framework is licensed under the GPL-2.0-or-later. Releases before 0.15 declared a proprietary license. A theme or plugin that ships the framework must be under a GPL-compatible license; this is also what the plugin directory of WordPress.org requires (see Distribution).

0.14

The release workflow tests in wp-test-env. consumer-release.yml used to install the release into the release site of wp-dev-env. Since 0.14 it uses wp-test-env, which starts a fresh WordPress for every test run and runs the browser tests with one Playwright worker per instance (see Releases and CI). Three things change in your project:

The input wp-dev-env-ref is now wp-test-env-ref. Rename it if your workflow sets it.

Your Playwright configuration receives the instance URLs in WP_BASE_URLS instead of one URL in WP_BASE_URL, and no E2E_BROWSER_HOST_RULES any more. Set workers to the number of URLs, pick the URL of each worker by TEST_PARALLEL_INDEX, and log in per worker instead of in a global setup. The configuration and fixtures.js of theme-dev-test show how.

tests/cli/run gets the name of a wp-test-env instance instead of a Compose service of wp-dev-env, and runs WP-CLI with ../wp-test-env/bin/wp <instance> … instead of docker compose exec.

0.13

The stylesheet moved to assets/styles.css. Each project now has an assets/ directory for everything that belongs to no PHP class (see Concepts), and the Tailwind stylesheet is the first file there. Move src/styles.css to assets/styles.css and make the paths in it relative to the new place: @source "./**/*.twig" becomes @source "../src/**/*.twig", and url(…) to files in src/ gets a ../src/ in front. A file left at src/styles.css is a build error in the manifest build and in the webpack helper, so it cannot be forgotten.

asset_url, asset_image and asset_svg are framework functions. 0.13 adds them for static assets. A template function of your own with one of these names is now a build error; rename it.

Scripts in src/ need a block or block support. An *.editor.js or *.view.js in src/ without a block or block support class of the same name next to it is now a build error. Before 0.13 the webpack helper built such a file, but the framework never loaded it.

0.12

Deleting a plugin deletes its data. Before 0.12, the framework left everything behind when a plugin was deleted. Since 0.12 it removes the posts of the plugin's post types, its terms, meta keys, settings, tables, cron events, technical options and caches (see Activation, deactivation and uninstallation). Back up the data before you delete a plugin whose data you want to keep.

A plugin must not have an uninstall.php. WordPress runs this file instead of the uninstall hook of the framework, so it is now a build error. Move its code into a method with #[OnUninstall].

0.11

link_attributes is a framework function. 0.11 adds the template function link_attributes() for links. A template function of your own with this name is now a build error; rename it.

Field classes name the class they belong to class. Since 0.11 fields describe the columns of tables as well as meta fields, so the first parameter of their constructors is called $class instead of $metaClass, and the getter getMetaClass() is now getClass(). Field classes written by hand or generated by wp-app-framework meta-fields pass the class positionally and keep working. Change the code only where it names the argument (new IntField(metaClass: EventDetails::class, …) becomes new IntField(class: EventDetails::class, …)) or calls getMetaClass().

0.10

Inner blocks are declared with #[InnerBlocks]. Before 0.10, #[Block] had one argument for containers, allowedBlocks, with block names as strings. 0.10 adds templates, locks and more for containers (see Container blocks); they live in an attribute of their own, #[InnerBlocks], and allowedBlocks moved there as allowed. Blocks are named so that your IDE can resolve them: blocks of your own by class, core blocks by CoreBlock.

Before	Since 0.10
#[Block('section', …, allowedBlocks: ['hero', 'core/paragraph'])]	#[Block('section', …)] and #[InnerBlocks(allowed: [Hero::class, CoreBlock::Paragraph])]
usesContext: ['sections/…'] for context of your own blocks	#[ProvidesContext] on the attribute and a render() parameter with #[Context(Block::class, 'attribute')]

allowedBlocks is removed without alias, so PHP reports the unknown argument. The build reports a block name in your own namespace (name the block by class) and a core block named as string. Other blocks stay strings with their full name.

field() checks its path only in the editor. Before 0.10, a wrong path also threw on the front end. Since 0.10 field() returns an empty string outside the editor without looking at the path, so it costs nothing on the front end. A wrong path still fails when the block renders in the editor.

Every block has an inserter preview. Without #[Example] the inserter now previews a block with its default attributes. Add #[Example(false)] to a block that should show none.

0.9

Each theme and plugin declares a namespace. Before 0.9, block names carried their namespace in #[Block] (sections/hero), REST controllers named their full REST namespace (sections/v1), and settings options were named after the slug, the directory name of the theme or plugin. The directory name changes when a theme is installed under another name, and its settings would be lost with it. Since 0.9 the namespace in composer.json names everything content and data refer to (see Concepts).

Add the namespace to composer.json. Use the namespace your blocks already have, so posts, templates and patterns keep working unchanged:

"extra": { "wp-app-framework": { "namespace": "sections" } }

Then change your code:

Before	Since 0.9
#[Block('sections/hero', …)]	#[Block('hero', …)]
allowedBlocks: ['sections/hero', 'core/paragraph']	allowedBlocks: ['hero', 'core/paragraph']
registerControl( 'sections/hero', … ), also registerPanel() and registerToolbarButton()	registerControl( 'hero', … )
#[RestController('sections/v1', …)]	#[RestController('v1', …)]

The build reports a missing namespace, a block name with / and an unknown own block in allowedBlocks; the register functions warn in the console about names with a namespace. Block markup in templates, parts and patterns keeps the full names.

Settings options are named after the namespace. The option of a settings group is now {namespace}_{name} instead of {slug}_{name}, with _ instead of -. If the two differ – the theme my-theme with the namespace sections stores the group general in sections_general instead of my_theme_general – the saved settings are not moved. Copy them once, for example with WP-CLI: wp option get my_theme_general --format=json | wp option update sections_general --format=json.

0.8

The build checks block templates, template parts and patterns. Before 0.8 the build looked at your PHP classes only. Mistakes in the block markup of your theme – a misspelled attribute, a value outside an enum, HTML in a block without a postContent field – went unnoticed, and WordPress dropped what it could not use. Since 0.8 the build checks these files against your blocks (see Checking templates, parts and patterns).

A theme or child theme that built fine with 0.7 may now fail with errors in templates/, parts/ or patterns/. Each error names the file, the line and the block; fix the markup as the message says. Two errors need more than a fix in place: PHP code inside the block comment of one of your blocks in a pattern (write the attributes as plain JSON), and a container of your theme without content that holds content blocks in a template part or a pattern with a single top-level block (give it #[Supports(contentRole: true)]).

0.7

Template functions that wrap WordPress functions start with wp_. Before 0.7 a template could call post_title() or attachment_image(), and nothing showed that these were WordPress functions rather than framework functions or functions of the theme. 0.7 gives all of them the prefix wp_ and adds many more (see WordPress functions).

The old names are removed without aliases. A template that still uses one fails to compile with an unknown function, so you won't miss any. Rename them in your templates:

Before	Since 0.7
attachment_image()	wp_attachment_image()
post_url()	wp_post_url()
post_title()	wp_post_title()
term_url()	wp_term_url()
term_name()	wp_term_name()
user_name()	wp_user_name()

If your own template functions use one of the new wp_ names, rename them as well: a name the framework already uses is a build error.

0.3

Child themes override theme templates in overrides/{theme}/ instead of src/. Since 0.3 a child theme can have code of its own and boot its own framework instance with ChildTheme::boot() (see Child themes). Its src/ directory now belongs to that instance and can no longer hold overrides of the parent theme.

Move each override from the child theme's src/ to overrides/{theme}/, keeping the path. For the parent theme my-theme, src/Block/Hero/Hero.twig becomes overrides/my-theme/Block/Hero/Hero.twig (see Twig templates).

0.2

The init action is named after the consumer. Since 0.2 plugins can use the framework next to a theme, and each runs its own instance. The single action wp_app_framework/init could not tell them apart, so it became wp_app_framework/init/{slug} (see Boot and modes).

Replace add_action('wp_app_framework/init', …) with the action of the instance you mean, for example wp_app_framework/init/my-theme.
description: From 1.0 on, the consumer API only grows within a major version: nothing is renamed, removed or changed in behavior, and a theme built against 1.0 keeps working with 1.9. Before 1.0, a minor version may still break the API. This page lists every such change, why it was made, and what you need to change in your theme or plugin. The documentation is published for each minor version. The version switcher in the navigation bar shows the documentation of other versions, so you can compare the old and the new state.
